import HodgeComputer.Constructions.FiniteAlgebra.RegularSpecialization
import Mathlib.Data.Complex.Basic
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Localization.Integer
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Localization.FractionRing
import Mathlib.RingTheory.MvPolynomial.Homogeneous
import Mathlib.Tactic.Ring
import Mathlib.Tactic.FinCases
import Mathlib.Tactic.FieldSimp
import Mathlib.Tactic.Choose
import Mathlib.Tactic.NormNum

noncomputable section
namespace HoldoutQ2.Clearing
open MvPolynomial
abbrev Parameters := MvPolynomial (Fin 2) ℂ
abbrev BasePoly := MvPolynomial (Fin 6) ℂ

def xa : BasePoly := X 0 * X 1

def goodParameters (k : ℂ) : Parameters →+* ℂ := eval₂Hom (RingHom.id ℂ) ![k^2,k]
def goodBase (k : ℂ) : BasePoly →+* ℂ := eval₂Hom (RingHom.id ℂ) ![1,1,0,k^2,k,0]

variable {k : ℂ}

/-- An encoding of (xa)^n p(b/a,d/c), including its full evaluation law. -/
structure HomogeneousDatum (p : Parameters) (n : ℕ) (H : BasePoly) : Prop where
  homogeneous : H.IsHomogeneous (2 * n)
  evaluation : ∀ {K : Type} [Field K] [Algebra ℂ K] (v : Fin 6 → K),
    v 0 ≠ 0 → v 1 ≠ 0 →
    eval₂ (algebraMap ℂ K) v H = (v 0 * v 1)^n *
      eval₂ (algebraMap ℂ K) ![v 3 / v 0, v 4 / v 1] p

theorem ac_homogeneous : xa.IsHomogeneous 2 :=
  (isHomogeneous_X ℂ 0).mul (isHomogeneous_X ℂ 1)

theorem homogeneousDatum_C (r : ℂ) : HomogeneousDatum (C r) 0 (C r) where
  homogeneous := isHomogeneous_C _ r
  evaluation := by intros; simp

theorem HomogeneousDatum.add {p q : Parameters} {n m : ℕ} {H J : BasePoly}
    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) (hq : HomogeneousDatum q m J) :
    HomogeneousDatum (p + q) (n + m) (H * xa^m + J * xa^n) where
  homogeneous := by
    have h1 := hp.homogeneous.mul (ac_homogeneous.pow m)
    have h2 := hq.homogeneous.mul (ac_homogeneous.pow n)
    convert h1.add (by simpa only [Nat.add_comm] using h2) using 1 <;> omega
  evaluation := by
    intro K _ _ v ha hc
    simp only [eval₂_add, eval₂_mul, eval₂_pow, xa, eval₂_X]
    rw [hp.evaluation v ha hc, hq.evaluation v ha hc]
    simp only [pow_add]
    ring

theorem HomogeneousDatum.mul_X {p : Parameters} {n : ℕ} {H : BasePoly}
    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) (j : Fin 2) :
    ∃ J, HomogeneousDatum (p * X j) (n + 1) J := by
  fin_cases j
  · refine ⟨H * (X 3 * X 1), ?_⟩
    constructor
    · have hh := hp.homogeneous.mul ((isHomogeneous_X ℂ 3).mul (isHomogeneous_X ℂ 1))
      convert hh using 1 <;> omega
    · intro K _ _ v ha hc
      simp only [eval₂_mul, eval₂_X, Matrix.cons_val, hp.evaluation v ha hc, pow_succ]
      norm_num [Matrix.cons_val, Fin.isValue]
      field_simp [ha, hc]
      <;> ring
  · refine ⟨H * (X 4 * X 0), ?_⟩
    constructor
    · have hh := hp.homogeneous.mul ((isHomogeneous_X ℂ 4).mul (isHomogeneous_X ℂ 0))
      convert hh using 1 <;> omega
    · intro K _ _ v ha hc
      simp only [eval₂_mul, eval₂_X, Matrix.cons_val, hp.evaluation v ha hc, pow_succ]
      norm_num [Matrix.cons_val, Fin.isValue]
      field_simp [ha, hc]
      <;> ring

theorem exists_homogeneousDatum (p : Parameters) : ∃ n H, HomogeneousDatum p n H := by
  induction p using MvPolynomial.induction_on with
  | C r => exact ⟨0, C r, homogeneousDatum_C r⟩
  | add p q hp hq =>
      obtain ⟨n, H, hH⟩ := hp
      obtain ⟨m, J, hJ⟩ := hq
      exact ⟨n + m, H * xa^m + J * xa^n, hH.add hJ⟩
  | mul_X p j hp =>
      obtain ⟨n, H, hH⟩ := hp
      obtain ⟨J, hJ⟩ := hH.mul_X j
      exact ⟨n + 1, J, hJ⟩

theorem HomogeneousDatum.raise {p : Parameters} {n : ℕ} {H : BasePoly}
    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) (k : ℕ) :
    HomogeneousDatum p (n + k) (H * xa^k) where
  homogeneous := by
    convert hp.homogeneous.mul (ac_homogeneous.pow k) using 1 <;> omega
  evaluation := by
    intro K _ _ v ha hc
    simp only [eval₂_mul, eval₂_pow, xa, eval₂_X, hp.evaluation v ha hc, pow_add]
    ring

theorem HomogeneousDatum.goodBase {p : Parameters} {n : ℕ} {H : BasePoly}
    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) : goodBase k H = goodParameters k p := by
  have he := hp.evaluation (K := ℂ) ![1,1,0,k^2,k,0] (by change (1:ℂ) ≠ 0; norm_num) (by change (1:ℂ) ≠ 0; norm_num)
  simpa [HoldoutQ2.Clearing.goodBase, goodParameters] using he

theorem exists_uniform_homogeneousDatum {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (p : ι → Parameters) : ∃ (n : ℕ) (H : ι → BasePoly), ∀ i, HomogeneousDatum (p i) n (H i) := by
  classical
  choose n H hh using fun i => exists_homogeneousDatum (p i)
  let N := ∑ i, n i
  refine ⟨N, fun i => H i * xa ^ (N - n i), ?_⟩
  intro i
  have hi : n i ≤ N := Finset.single_le_sum (fun j _ => Nat.zero_le (n j)) (Finset.mem_univ i)
  simpa only [Nat.add_sub_of_le hi] using (hh i).raise (N - n i)

/-- A finite family of regular coefficients has a good common denominator. -/
theorem regular_common_denominator {ι : Type*} [Finite ι]
    (z : ι → RegularSpecialization.Coefficients (goodParameters k)) :
    ∃ q : Parameters, goodParameters k q ≠ 0 ∧ ∃ p : ι → Parameters,
      ∀ i, algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients (goodParameters k)) (p i) =
        algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients (goodParameters k)) q * z i := by
  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ := IsLocalization.exist_integer_multiples_of_finite
    (RegularSpecialization.denominators (goodParameters k)) z
  choose p hp using hq
  refine ⟨q, q.property, p, ?_⟩
  intro i
  simpa [Algebra.smul_def] using hp i

/-- Matching-degree numerator/denominator encodings preserving good specialization. -/
theorem regular_uniform_homogeneous_clearing {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (z : ι → RegularSpecialization.Coefficients (goodParameters k)) :
    ∃ (n : ℕ) (q : Parameters) (p : ι → Parameters) (D : BasePoly) (N : ι → BasePoly),
      HomogeneousDatum q n D ∧ goodBase k D ≠ 0 ∧
      (∀ i, HomogeneousDatum (p i) n (N i)) ∧
      (∀ i, algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients (goodParameters k)) (p i) =
        algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients (goodParameters k)) q * z i) := by
  classical
  obtain ⟨q, hq, p, hp⟩ := regular_common_denominator z
  obtain ⟨n, H, hh⟩ := exists_uniform_homogeneousDatum (fun i : Option ι => i.elim q p)
  refine ⟨n, q, p, H none, fun i => H (some i), hh none, ?_, fun i => hh (some i), hp⟩
  rw [(hh none).goodBase (k := k)]
  exact hq

end HoldoutQ2.Clearing

#print axioms HoldoutQ2.Clearing.regular_uniform_homogeneous_clearing

  homogeneous : H.IsHomogeneous (2 * n)

    v 1 ≠ 0 → v 2 ≠ 0 →
    eval₂ (algebraMap ℚ K) v H = (v 1 * v 2)^n *
      eval₂ (algebraMap ℚ K) ![v 4 / v 1, v 5 / v 2] p

  (isHomogeneous_X ℚ 1).mul (isHomogeneous_X ℚ 2)

  homogeneous := isHomogeneous_C _ r
  evaluation := by intros; simp

    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) (hq : HomogeneousDatum q m J) :

  homogeneous := by
    have h1 := hp.homogeneous.mul (ac_homogeneous.pow m)
    have h2 := hq.homogeneous.mul (ac_homogeneous.pow n)
    convert h1.add (by simpa only [Nat.add_comm] using h2) using 1 <;> omega
  evaluation := by
    intro K _ _ v ha hc
    simp only [eval₂_add, eval₂_mul, eval₂_pow, ac, eval₂_X]
    rw [hp.evaluation v ha hc, hq.evaluation v ha hc]
    simp only [pow_add]
    ring

    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) (j : Fin 2) :
    ∃ J, HomogeneousDatum (p * X j) (n + 1) J := by
  fin_cases j
  · refine ⟨H * (X 4 * X 2), ?_⟩
    constructor
    · have hh := hp.homogeneous.mul ((isHomogeneous_X ℚ 4).mul (isHomogeneous_X ℚ 2))

    · intro K _ _ v ha hc

  · refine ⟨H * (X 5 * X 1), ?_⟩

    · intro K _ _ v ha hc

  | C r => exact ⟨0, C r, homogeneousDatum_C r⟩

  | mul_X p j hp =>
      obtain ⟨n, H, hH⟩ := hp
      obtain ⟨J, hJ⟩ := hH.mul_X j

  homogeneous := by
    convert hp.homogeneous.mul (ac_homogeneous.pow k) using 1 <;> omega
  evaluation := by
    intro K _ _ v ha hc
    simp only [eval₂_mul, eval₂_pow, ac, eval₂_X, hp.evaluation v ha hc, pow_add]
    ring

theorem HomogeneousDatum.goodBase {p : Parameters} {n : ℕ} {H : BasePoly}
    (hp : HomogeneousDatum p n H) : goodBase H = goodParameters p := by
  have he := hp.evaluation (K := ℚ) ![0,1,1,0,1,2] (by change (1:ℚ) ≠ 0; norm_num) (by change (1:ℚ) ≠ 0; norm_num)

theorem regular_common_denominator {ι : Type*} [Finite ι]
    (z : ι → RegularSpecialization.Coefficients goodParameters) :
    ∃ q : Parameters, goodParameters q ≠ 0 ∧ ∃ p : ι → Parameters,
      ∀ i, algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients goodParameters) (p i) =
        algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients goodParameters) q * z i := by
  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ := IsLocalization.exist_integer_multiples_of_finite
    (RegularSpecialization.denominators goodParameters) z
  choose p hp using hq
  refine ⟨q, q.property, p, ?_⟩

  simpa [Algebra.smul_def] using hp i

/-- Matching-degree numerator/denominator encodings preserving good specialization. -/
theorem regular_uniform_homogeneous_clearing {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (z : ι → RegularSpecialization.Coefficients goodParameters) :
    ∃ (n : ℕ) (q : Parameters) (p : ι → Parameters) (D : BasePoly) (N : ι → BasePoly),
      HomogeneousDatum q n D ∧ goodBase D ≠ 0 ∧
      (∀ i, HomogeneousDatum (p i) n (N i)) ∧
      (∀ i, algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients goodParameters) (p i) =
        algebraMap Parameters (RegularSpecialization.Coefficients goodParameters) q * z i) := by
  classical
  obtain ⟨q, hq, p, hp⟩ := regular_common_denominator z
  obtain ⟨n, H, hh⟩ := exists_uniform_homogeneousDatum (fun i : Option ι => i.elim q p)
  refine ⟨n, q, p, H none, fun i => H (some i), hh none, ?_, fun i => hh (some i), hp⟩
  rw [(hh none).goodBase]
  exact hq

      φ (v 1 * v 2) ![v 4/v 1,v 5/v 2] hB hG
    simpa only [hC, φ, coe_eval₂Hom] using h

theorem exists_homogeneousDatum (p : Parameters) : ∃ n H, HomogeneousDatum p n H := by
  exact ⟨p.totalDegree, _, homogeneousDatum_of_degree p p.totalDegree le_rfl⟩

theorem HomogeneousDatum.goodBase {p : Parameters} {n : ℕ} {H : BasePoly}

  have he := hp.evaluation (K := ℚ) ![0,1,1,0,1,2] (by change (1:ℚ) ≠ 0; norm_num) (by change (1:ℚ) ≠ 0; norm_num)

# 1. From invariant cohomology to rational certificates

[Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: explicit constructions](#technical-information/explicit-constructions)

The geometric objective is to support the involution-invariant part of \(H^{4}\) of a smooth sextic fourfold on a divisor. The certificate equation translates this objective into an exact identity involving rational functions. Its advantage is that a proposed solution can be verified independently of the argument or numerical experiment that produced it. Its difficulty is concentrated in constructing the denominator.

## The hypersurface and its targets

Write \(Z=(X_{0},X_{1},X_{2},Y_{0},Y_{1},Y_{2})\), let \(\tau (X,Y)=(X,-Y)\), and fix a homogeneous sextic \(F\) over a characteristic-zero field \(k\subset \mathbb C\) such that \(F(X,-Y)=F(X,Y)\) and \(X=V(F)\subset \mathbb P^{5}\) is smooth. A polynomial is **\(Y\)-even** or **\(Y\)-odd** according to the parity of its total degree in the three \(Y\) variables. Explicit records usually use \(k=\mathbb Q\) or a stated number field. Globally \(Y\)-even is the standing hypothesis; invariance under each individual coordinate sign change is a stronger condition used by particular constructions. The central target list uses integers \(q\in \{1,2\}\); several constructions extend to other positive \(q\) with the same conventions.

We use Griffiths's residue theorem as a foundational input: residues of forms with pole order at most \(q+1\) span \(F^{4-q}H^{4}(X,\mathbb C)_{\mathrm{prim}}\), and their leading Hodge-graded quotient is the degree-\(6\cdot q\) piece of \(S/J(F)\), where \(S=\mathbb C[Z]\) and \(J(F)\) is the Jacobian ideal. This holds for \(0\le q\le 4\). Lower-pole numerators can be multiplied by \(F\) to put all forms over \(F^{q+1}\). The residue and filtration statements, including their projective normalization, are presented in [Diamond, Theorem 2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29157v2#S2).

Let \(\Omega =\iota _\epsilon (dZ_{0}\wedge \cdots \wedge dZ_{5})\), where \(\epsilon =\sum _{i} Z_{i}\partial /\partial Z_{i}\) is the Euler field. Since \(\tau^{*}\Omega =-\Omega \), the Griffiths form

\[
\begin{gathered}
\omega _A = A\cdot \Omega /F^{q+1},       \operatorname{deg} A = 6\cdot q,
\end{gathered}
\]

has invariant residue when \(A\) is \(Y\)-odd. Its residue lies in \(F^{4-q}H^{4}(X,\mathbb C)_{\mathrm{prim}}\). In particular, \(q=1\) presents the invariant (3,1) classes; \(q=2\) presents the invariant Hodge-filtration level \(F^{2}\) and can also contain a contribution of type (3,1). The ambient class is the square of the hyperplane class and is already algebraic. There is no invariant (4,0) part, because \(\Omega \) changes sign. The desired generalized Hodge statement is

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{4}(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau  \subset  N^{1}H^{4}(X,\mathbb Q).
\end{gathered}
\]

Here \(N^{1}\) denotes the rational subspace generated by classes vanishing off divisors. It is a Hodge substructure, by the Gysin description proved in Chapter 3. Solving all \(Y\)-odd targets for \(q=1,2\) puts the invariant \(F^{2}\) part in \(N^{1}\otimes \mathbb C\). Complex conjugation then puts its conjugate there too, and \(F^{2}\) plus its conjugate exhausts the invariant \(H^{4}\). Taking supports for a finite spanning set gives one finite union of divisors supporting everything. Monomials form a convenient input basis, but targets may be arbitrary \(Y\)-odd homogeneous polynomials.

There is no loss in seeking an ambient equation \(D\) for such a support. The Lefschetz theorem on Picard groups gives \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\mathbb Z[\mathcal O_X(1)]\), so an effective divisor has class \(\mathcal O_X(e)\) with \(e>0\). Its section lifts to a homogeneous polynomial \(D\) because \(H^{1}(\mathbb P^{5},\mathcal O(e-6))=0\) in the restriction sequence. The lift is not a multiple of \(F\). A \(\tau \)-stable support can be represented by the even polynomial \(D\cdot \tau (D)\), with repetitions allowed.

## The key equation

For \(v=(v_{0},\ldots ,v_{5})\), set \(v(F)=\sum _{i}v_{i}\partial _{i}F\) and \(\operatorname{div}(v)=\sum _{i}\partial _{i}v_{i}\). A certificate for \((F,q,A)\) is a rational field with homogeneous components of degree \(6\cdot q-5\), with every denominator coprime to \(F\), satisfying

\[
\begin{gathered}
F^{q+1} \mid  K_A(v),       K_A(v) \coloneqq  A - q\cdot v(F) + F\cdot \operatorname{div}(v).
\end{gathered}
\]

Divisibility is in the local ring \(k[Z]_{(F)}\): clear the denominators, which are units there, and check polynomial divisibility. The field can be chosen with \(Y\)-odd components \(v_{0},v_{1},v_{2}\) and \(Y\)-even components \(v_{3},v_{4},v_{5}\). Averaging with respect to \(\tau \) enforces these parities without changing the target.

The bridge to geometry is the rational four-form \(\beta =-\iota _v\Omega /F^q\). Homogeneity makes it a projective form: its weight is zero and contraction with \(\epsilon \) is zero. Its differential satisfies

\[
\begin{gathered}
\omega _A - d\beta  = K_A(v)\cdot\Omega /F^{q+1}.
\end{gathered}
\]

To prove the identity, put \(\mathrm{vol}=dZ_{0}\wedge \cdots \wedge dZ_{5}\). Cartan's formula and \(\operatorname{deg} v_{i}=6\cdot q-5\) give

\[
\begin{gathered}
d(\iota _v\Omega )=\operatorname{div}(v)\cdot\Omega -6\cdot q\iota _{v}\mathrm{vol},\\
dF\wedge \iota _v\Omega =v(F)\cdot\Omega -6\cdot F\iota _{v}\mathrm{vol}.
\end{gathered}
\]

Applying the quotient rule to \(\beta \) cancels the two terms containing \(\iota _{v}\mathrm{vol}\) and yields the displayed formula. The same calculation in \(\mathbb P^{n}\) for \(d=\operatorname{deg} F\) uses \(\operatorname{deg} A=d\cdot(q+1)-(n+1)\) and \(\operatorname{deg} v_{i}=d\cdot q-n\), and replaces \(6\cdot q\) by \(d\cdot q\).

The key equation therefore says that \(\omega _A-d\beta \) has no pole along \(X\). On the complement of the denominator locus, the residue of an exact form and the residue of a form regular across \(X\) both vanish in cohomology, proving sufficiency. The prescribed-support theorem below proves the converse, together with an auxiliary pole bound, without leaving a separate algebraization step implicit. Diamond's Section 2 gives another necessity argument with a bound along \(X\); that bound alone does not impose simple poles along the auxiliary divisor.

## One denominator and the normalized equations

Every finite rational tuple has a common denominator. We may choose it \(Y\)-even, multiplying by its involution conjugate when necessary, and write

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=N/D,       \operatorname{deg} N_{i}=\operatorname{deg}(D)+6\cdot q-5,       \operatorname{gcd}(D,F)=1.
\end{gathered}
\]

A common denominator introduces no restriction on certificate existence. The quotient rule gives

\[
K_A(N/D) = [D\cdot(A\cdot D-q\cdot N(F)) + F\cdot(D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D))]/D^{2}.
\]

For this fixed \(D\), existence is equivalent to the following polynomial system:

\[
\begin{gathered}
E_{1}: q\cdot N(F)=A\cdot D,\\
E_{2}: D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D) \in  (F^q).
\end{gathered}
\]

The forward implication is an Euler normalization, not an extra ansatz. Indeed, the key equation first forces \(A\cdot D-q\cdot N(F)=F\cdot H\) for a polynomial \(H\). Replacing \(N\) by \(N'=N+H\epsilon /(6\cdot q)\) makes \(E_{1}\) exact. Since \(\operatorname{deg} H=\operatorname{deg}(D)+6\cdot q-6\), Euler's identity also gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N')-N'(D) = D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D)+D\cdot H,
\end{gathered}
\]

which is precisely the expression already required to lie in \((F^q)\). Degrees and parities are preserved.

For fixed \(D\), both equations are linear in the coefficients of \(N\). One can compare coefficients after reducing \(E_{2}\) modulo \(F^q\), or introduce a quotient polynomial and impose an exact identity. Thus the unrestricted fixed-denominator question is finite linear algebra. Restricting \(N\) to a convenient smaller space changes that question and requires a separate completeness argument.

A certificate is **strict** when \(K_A(v)=0\) as a rational function. In normalized form this means \(E_{1}\) holds and \(E_{2}\) vanishes identically, rather than merely modulo \(F^q\). Strictness is a property of the chosen field; ordinary solvability does not require it.

## Euler freedom and denominator gauges

For every homogeneous rational \(\phi \) of degree \(6\cdot q-6\),

\[
\begin{gathered}
q(\phi\cdot\epsilon )(F)=6\cdot q\phi F=F\cdot \operatorname{div}(\phi\cdot\epsilon ).
\end{gathered}
\]

Consequently \(v\) and \(v+\phi\cdot\epsilon \) have the same \(K_A\). An Euler shift preserves strictness as well as ordinary solvability. With \(\phi  Y\)-odd it also preserves parity. The preceding normalization uses \(\phi =H/(6\cdot q\cdot D)\), whose poles remain legal.

There are also formally invisible Euler fields with poles on \(X\), such as \((P/F)\epsilon \) for \(\operatorname{deg} P=6\cdot q\). These are not legal certificate fields: the coprimality requirement forbids their denominator. A coefficient search which admits \(D\) proportional to \(F\) can therefore detect spurious solutions. Homogeneity and small residual alone do not certify legality.

One further gauge is useful for sextic denominators at \(q=1\):

\[
\begin{gathered}
(D,N) \mapsto  (D+t\cdot F, N+t\cdot A\cdot \epsilon /6).
\end{gathered}
\]

It preserves \(E_{1}\) and \(E_{2}\) modulo \(F\), and \(V(F,D+t\cdot F)=V(F,D)\). It need not preserve strictness, since it changes the rational field itself. Coprimality must still be checked. This gauge is distinct from adding an Euler field to a fixed \(v\).

Indeed, put \(B_D(N)=D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D)\). For \(q=1\) and \(\operatorname{deg} D=6\), the shifted numerator has \(N'(F)=A(D+t\cdot F)\). Euler's identity gives \(\operatorname{div}(A\cdot \epsilon /6)=2\cdot A\) and \((A\cdot \epsilon /6)(D)=A\cdot D\). Expanding then gives

\[
B_{D+t\cdot F}(N+t\cdot A\cdot \epsilon /6) = B_D(N)+t\cdot F(\operatorname{div} N+t\cdot A),
\]

using \(E_{1}\) to cancel the remaining terms. This proves precisely the stated modulo-\(F\) invariance.

## Prescribed support and pole multiplicity

The support of a divisor ignores multiplicities; a rational primitive does not. These facts must be kept separate when fixing a denominator.

**Prescribed-support theorem.** Let \(D\) be nonconstant, homogeneous, \(Y\)-even and coprime to \(F\), and let \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\) be a squarefree equation of \(V(D)\). For \(1\le q\le 4\), the following statements are equivalent:

1. \(\operatorname{Res}_X(\omega _A)\) vanishes on \(X\setminus V(D)\).
2. A certificate exists with poles confined to \(V(D)\).
3. A certificate exists with denominator \(D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\).

In particular, \(D^q\) also suffices. Over the field of definition of \(F,A,D\), the numerator can be chosen over that same field. The field can be chosen with the prescribed component parities. With the even presentation \(D^q\), its numerator has those same parities; a squarefree equation \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\) can itself be odd, in which case its numerator transforms accordingly. No smoothness or normal-crossing hypothesis is imposed on \(V(D)\) or its intersection with \(X\). Without a field-parity requirement, the same equivalence applies to arbitrary homogeneous \(D\).

We prove the slightly more general statement for a smooth degree-\(d\) hypersurface \(X\subset P=\mathbb P^{n}\), with \(n\ge 2, 1\le q\le n-1\) and \(\operatorname{deg} A=d\cdot(q+1)-(n+1)\). Put \(R=V(D_{\mathrm{red}}), e=\operatorname{deg} D_{\mathrm{red}}\), and work over \(\mathbb C\) until the final linear descent. We use unshifted de Rham complexes, with differential forms in degrees \(0,\ldots ,n\).

The external inputs are the following standard facts about mixed Hodge modules and projective space. They are stated here to specify exactly what the proof uses.

- Localization along a reduced divisor \(T\) carries a Hodge filtration \(\mathcal F\) with \(\mathcal F_{-1}\mathcal O_P(*T)=0\) and \(\mathcal F_{k}\mathcal O_P(*T)\subset \mathcal O_P((k+1)T)\) for \(k\ge 0\); equality holds when \(T\) is smooth. Inclusions and quotients of these filtered modules are strict. See [Mustaţă–Popa, Hodge ideals, equation (0.1) and §§4–7](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~mpopa/papers/SI.pdf).
- Projective direct image is strict: for a filtered mixed Hodge module \(M\) on projective \(P\), the map from the hypercohomology of \(\mathcal F^p\operatorname{DR}(M)\) to that of \(\operatorname{DR}(M)\) is injective. Here its \(j\)-th term is \(\Omega ^{j}_P\otimes \mathcal F_{j-p}M\). See [Mustaţă–Popa, Hodge ideals for \(\mathbb Q\)-divisors, §1 and equation (1.1)](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/jep.94.pdf).
- Algebraic de Rham comparison identifies localization with the derived direct image from the divisor complement; this is the comparison input used in [Diamond, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29157v2#S2.SS3). Bott vanishing gives \(H^{i}(P,\Omega ^{j}_P(b))=0\) for \(b>0\) and \(i>0\), as recalled in [Hodge ideals, §25](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~mpopa/papers/SI.pdf); line bundles on \(\mathbb P^{n}\) also have zero \(H^{1}\) for \(n\ge 2\).

**Proof.** Set

\[
\begin{gathered}
M=\mathcal O_P(*(X+R))/\mathcal O_P(*R).
\end{gathered}
\]

The residue comparison is \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,\operatorname{DR}(M))\cong H^{n-1}(X\setminus R,\mathbb C)\), with the usual residue Tate shift. To see the shift, work first on \(P\setminus R\) with a local normal coordinate \(t\) for the smooth \(X\). Modulo regular forms, all higher normal poles are exact and the only normal de Rham class is \(\mathrm dt/t\), one degree higher than the corresponding class on \(X\). Localization along \(R\) extends this residue identification to \(P\). Since \(X\) is smooth, \(\omega _A\) belongs to the top term of \(\mathcal F^{n-q}\operatorname{DR}(M)\): it comes from \(\mathcal F_q\mathcal O_P(*X)=\mathcal O_P((q+1)X)\). If its residue vanishes, strictness of projective direct image says that its class already vanishes in \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,\mathcal F^{n-q}\operatorname{DR}(M))\). This is the only step that requires more than unfiltered de Rham exactness.

For \(n-q\le j\le n\) put \(a_j=j-n+q+1\) and introduce the finite complex

\[
\begin{gathered}
K^{j}=\Omega ^{j}_P\otimes [\mathcal O_P(a_j(X+R))/\mathcal O_P(a_jR)],\\
K^{j}=0 \;\text{for}\; j<n-q.
\end{gathered}
\]

Differentiation increases each pole order by at most one, so it gives the differential of \(K^{\bullet} \). The Hodge pole bound provides a map of complexes \(\mathcal F^{n-q}\operatorname{DR}(M)\to K^{\bullet} \). To check this on quotients, a filtered representative has poles at most \(a_j\) along both \(X\) and \(R\). A representative lying in \(\mathcal O_P(*R)\) therefore lies in \(\mathcal O_P(a_jR)\). Strictness identifies precisely those representatives with \(\mathcal F_{a_j-1}\mathcal O_P(*R)\), so the quotient map is well defined. Consequently the class of \(\omega _A\) is zero in \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,K^{\bullet} )\).

Each \(K^{j}\) has zero higher cohomology. Indeed, in

\[
\begin{gathered}
0 \to  \Omega ^{j}_P(a_jR) \to  \Omega ^{j}_P(a_j(X+R)) \to  K^{j} \to  0
\end{gathered}
\]

both twists are positive because \(a_j\ge 1\) and \(e>0\). Bott vanishing and the long exact sequence give the claim. Hence \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,K^{\bullet} )\) is computed by global sections. The zero class of the top section \(\omega _A\) supplies a global section \(\overline{\beta }\) of \(K^{n-1}\) with \(d\overline{\beta }=\omega _A\). The same sequence in degree \(n-1\), and \(H^{1}(P,\Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot R))=0\), lift it to

\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta  \in  H^{0}(P,\Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot X+q\cdot R)).
\end{gathered}
\]

Thus \(\omega _A-d\beta \) has poles only on \(R\). In particular, the primitive has at most \(q\)-fold poles along every component of \(R\) and along \(X\), with no added support.

It remains to obtain the vector field, rather than merely assert that a rational form can be represented. The identity \(\Omega ^{n-1}_P\cong T_P(-n-1)\) and the twisted Euler sequence give

\[
0 \to  \mathcal O_P(q(d+e)-n-1) \to  \mathcal O_P(q(d+e)-n)^{n+1} \to  \Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot X+q\cdot R) \to  0.
\]

The left term has zero \(H^{1}\). Therefore \(\beta \) is represented by a homogeneous polynomial tuple \(N\) of degree \(q(d+e)-n\):

\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta =-\iota _N\Omega /(F^q\cdot D_{\mathrm{red}}^q).
\end{gathered}
\]

With \(v=N/D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\), the differential identity proved above converts the absence of an \(X\)-pole into the key equation. This proves \(1\Longrightarrow 3\). The implication \(3\Longrightarrow 2\) is immediate, and \(2\Longrightarrow 1\) is the residue argument already given. Multiplying \(N\) by \((D/D_{\mathrm{red}})^q\) gives the prescribed denominator \(D^q\). Averaging the field under \(\tau \) preserves this even denominator and the target, and enforces the component parities. It can also retain \(D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\), since stability of its reduced support implies \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\circ \tau =\pm D_{\mathrm{red}}\). Finally, the fixed-denominator normalized equations form a finite linear system over the original coefficient field. Consistency over \(\mathbb C\) implies consistency over that field by Gaussian elimination. ∎

This also proves the claimed necessity of certificates for an arbitrary divisor support: choose an ambient \(D\) cutting that divisor, apply the theorem, and use the resulting polynomial tuple. If the original coefficients lie in a smaller field, the descent argument below gives a certificate over that field, possibly with a different support. The proof bounds poles on a chosen support; it supplies no bound on the degree \(e\) of the support itself.

At **\(q=1\)**, therefore, existence over \(D\) is equivalent to existence over any \(D^{m}\). An exact failure of the full fixed-\(D\) linear system excludes every higher power of that \(D\). At **\(q=2\)**, the definitive test on its support uses \(D^{2}\). Failure over \(D\) alone need not exclude support.

The distinction is sharp. Set

\[
\begin{gathered}
D=X_{0}^{6}+X_{1}^{6}+X_{2}^{6},       E=Y_{0}^{6}+Y_{1}^{6}+Y_{2}^{6},       F=D+E,\\
A=X_{0}^{3}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{3}\cdot Y_{0}\cdot Y_{1}\cdot Y_{2},       q=2.
\end{gathered}
\]

Writing \(\epsilon _X\) and \(\epsilon _Y\) for the two block Euler fields, the strict certificate is

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=A(F\epsilon _X-D\cdot \epsilon _Y)/(12\cdot D^{2}).
\end{gathered}
\]

For the numerator \(N_{2}=A(F\epsilon _X-D\cdot \epsilon _Y)/12\), direct blockwise differentiation gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
2\cdot N_{2}(F)=A\cdot D^{2},       \operatorname{div} N_{2}=A\cdot F,       N_{2}(D^{2})=A\cdot F\cdot D^{2}.
\end{gathered}
\]

These identities prove both normalized equations, with \(E_{2}\) identically zero. The field has degree seven and the required parities. Fermat smoothness is immediate from its partial derivatives, and \(D\) is coprime to \(F\) because \(D\) and \(E\) involve disjoint variables and have no common factor.

There is no numerator over \(D\). To prove this without an ansatz, normalize \(E_{1}\) and average a hypothetical numerator over the six independent sixth-root coordinate scalings, projecting onto the character of \(A\). Both \(F\) and \(D\) are invariant, so this operation preserves the fixed denominator and the two equations. The retained monomials in \(N_{i}\) have exponent vector congruent modulo six to \((3,3,3,1,1,1)+e_{i}\). These six residues are all less than six and already sum to the required numerator degree thirteen. Thus \(N_{i}=c_{i}AZ_{i}\) is the entire surviving space, not a selected family. \(E_{1}\) forces \(c_{0}=c_{1}=c_{2}=1/12\) and \(c_{3}=c_{4}=c_{5}=0\). For this numerator, \(\operatorname{div} N=A\) and \(N(D)=A\cdot D/2\), so \(E_{2}\) is \(A\cdot D/2\). It is not divisible even by \(F\). This excludes every original numerator because normalization and averaging preserve existence.

These bounds leave the central search problem untouched: they do not bound the degree of the reduced support that must be found.

## Combining certificates and descending coefficients

For fixed \(F\) and \(q\), the equation is linear in the pair \((A,v)\). If \(v_j\) serves \(A_j\), then \(\sum _{j}c_j\cdot v_j\) serves \(\sum _{j}c_jA_j\). A product of the denominators supplies a common denominator, so supported target spaces add when supports are united. A decomposition into symmetry characters can therefore organize a search without requiring one denominator to serve every component separately.

In cleared form, certificates \((D,N,Q)\) for \(A\) and \((E,M,R)\) for \(B\) combine as

\[
D_{A+B}=DE,\qquad N_{A+B}=EN+DM,\qquad
Q_{A+B}=E^2Q+D^2R.
\]

The resulting defect is \(E^2\mathcal E_A+D^2\mathcal E_B=F^{q+1}(E^2Q+D^2R)\). Nonzero quotient terms therefore cause no obstruction to addition. Denominator legality is preserved by products, and for positive \(q\) each numerator has degree \(\deg D+\deg E+6q-5\).

If \(F\) and \(A\) are rational and \(v\) is defined over a number field \(K\), normalized trace gives a rational certificate:

\[
\begin{gathered}
v_\mathbb Q = \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(v)/[K:\mathbb Q].
\end{gathered}
\]

To prove descent, sum the conjugate fields over all embeddings of \(K\) into a normal closure. Differentiation commutes with each embedding, so each conjugate serves the same \(A\). Their average is Galois-invariant and hence rational. The product of the conjugate denominators is the norm, clears that average, and has degree \([K:\mathbb Q]\operatorname{deg} D\) before cancellation. Each factor is coprime to \(F\), so the norm remains legal. Homogeneity and parity are unchanged.

The same argument works for every finite extension \(K/k\) in characteristic zero. It also suffices to descend an initially complex certificate for data over \(k\). Fix its denominator degree and write the normalized equations in the finitely many coefficients of \(D,N\) and the \(E_{2}\) quotient. These are polynomial equations over \(k\). Legality is an open condition: at least one coefficient of the remainder of \(D\) modulo \(F\) is nonzero. Choose such a coefficient and invert it using one additional variable. A complex point of this finite polynomial system implies a point over an algebraic closure of \(k\), by the Nullstellensatz; its finitely many coordinates generate a finite extension. Trace then gives a certificate over \(k\). This proves descent of existence, without claiming to preserve an initially transcendental supporting equation.

For a bundled target \(A+cB\), with \(1,c\) linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the nondegenerate trace pairing supplies \(p\in K\) satisfying \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p\cdot c)=0\). Indeed, evaluation of that pairing on the independent vectors \(1,c\) defines a surjective linear map \(K\to \mathbb Q^{2}\). Applying trace to the certificate identity for \(p\cdot v\) shows that \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p\cdot v)\) serves \(A\). More generally a trace-dual basis extracts every rational component of an extension-field target. Trace over passive function fields appears in Chapter 2, where commutation with the relevant derivatives is proved for that setting.

For completeness, character averaging also has an explicit formula. Suppose a finite diagonal group acts by \(\gamma :Z_{i}\mapsto \gamma _{i}Z_{i}\), with \(F\circ \gamma =\mu _\gamma F\) and \(A\circ \gamma =\nu _\gamma A\). Define

\[
\begin{gathered}
(T_\gamma v)_{i}=\mu _\gamma (v_{i}\circ \gamma )/(\nu _\gamma \gamma _{i}).
\end{gathered}
\]

The chain rule gives \(K_A(T_\gamma v)=K_A(v)\circ \gamma /\nu _\gamma \). Thus averaging \(T_\gamma v\) preserves the certificate and projects onto the required character. A common denominator is the product of the conjugates, so its degree may grow by the group order. This does not justify imposing a single character on \(D\) at a previously chosen degree.

There is a useful exponent description when \(F\) contains all six pure sixth powers. Let \(L(F)\) be the lattice generated by differences of exponents in the support of \(F\). Diagonal substitutions preserving \(F\) up to scalar are exactly the characters of \(\mathbb Z^{6}/L(F)\). Modulo global scalar substitutions this is a finite group: the six pure powers force all \(\gamma _{i}^{6}\) to agree, and a common scalar makes them all one. Characters separate its exponent cosets at fixed degree. For a character field component, reduced numerator and denominator are both eigenvectors: the identity obtained by transforming their coprime quotient forces each factor to be carried to a scalar multiple of itself. Their characters differ by that of \(A\) times the \(i\)-th coordinate divided by the character of \(F\). This proves the support-coset rule without discarding rational fields, though averaging may increase degree.

For a full-support \(Y\)-even sextic, \(L(F)\) is exactly the lattice of vectors of total sum zero and even \(Y\)-sum. One inclusion follows from parity. Conversely, exponent differences realize all within-\(X\) and within-\(Y\) coordinate transfers, and also \(2(e_{X_{i}}-e_{Y_{j}})\); these generate that lattice. Hence all \(Y\)-odd targets of one degree belong to a single coset. Fine target-character decompositions are a property of structured \(F\), not an available simplification for general \(F\).

## Jacobian reduction and exact verification

Let \(J(F)=(\partial _{0}F,\ldots ,\partial _{5}F)\). If \(A=\sum _{i}G_{i}\partial _{i}F\), taking \(v=G/q\) gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
K_A(G/q)=F\cdot \operatorname{div}(G)/q.
\end{gathered}
\]

This lowers the pole order by one: modulo an exact form, \(\omega _A\) becomes \((\operatorname{div} G/q)\Omega /F^q\). Membership in \(J(F)\) therefore kills the leading Hodge-graded piece; it need not kill the whole residue class. For invariant \(q=1\) targets it does kill the class: the lower contribution would lie in the anti-invariant (4,0) space. Equivalently, after parity averaging, \(\operatorname{div}(G)\) is a \(Y\)-odd constant and hence zero.

For a concrete \(q=2\) example in our diagonal involution coordinates, take Fermat \(F\) and

\[
\begin{gathered}
A=6\cdot X_{0}^{6}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0},       G_{0}=X_{0}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0},       G_{i}=0 \;\text{for}\; i>0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Then \(A=\sum G_{i}\partial _{i}F\) is \(Y\)-odd and belongs to \(J(F)\), but one reduction gives the \(q=1\) numerator \(X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0}/2\). All of its exponents are at most four, so it is nonzero in the Fermat Jacobian ring \(\mathbb C[Z]/(Z_{0}^{5},\ldots ,Z_{5}^{5})\). Griffiths's graded isomorphism makes its (3,1) class nonzero. Thus the original \(q=2\) residue is nonzero, despite Jacobian membership. A complete reduction algorithm must retain this lower-pole target.

For an explicit field, clearing denominators reduces verification to polynomial identities and the homogeneity and coprimality conditions. A nonzero remainder is allowed when it is divisible by \(F^{q+1}\); strictness is a stronger sufficient condition. [Chapter 5](#technical-information/computation) gives the complete polynomial criterion.

# 1. From invariant cohomology to rational certificates

[Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: explicit constructions](#technical-information/explicit-constructions)

The geometric objective is to support the involution-invariant part of \(H^{4}\) of a smooth sextic fourfold on a divisor. The certificate equation translates this objective into an exact identity involving rational functions. Its advantage is that a proposed solution can be verified independently of the argument or numerical experiment that produced it. Its difficulty is concentrated in constructing the denominator.

## The hypersurface and its targets

Write \(Z=(X_{0},X_{1},X_{2},Y_{0},Y_{1},Y_{2})\), let \(\tau (X,Y)=(X,-Y)\), and fix a homogeneous sextic \(F\) over a characteristic-zero field \(k\subset \mathbb C\) such that \(F(X,-Y)=F(X,Y)\) and \(X=V(F)\subset \mathbb P^{5}\) is smooth. A polynomial is **\(Y\)-even** or **\(Y\)-odd** according to the parity of its total degree in the three \(Y\) variables. Explicit records usually use \(k=\mathbb Q\) or a stated number field. Globally \(Y\)-even is the standing hypothesis; invariance under each individual coordinate sign change is a stronger condition used by particular constructions. The central target list uses integers \(q\in \{1,2\}\); several constructions extend to other positive \(q\) with the same conventions.

We use Griffiths's residue theorem as a foundational input: residues of forms with pole order at most \(q+1\) span \(F^{4-q}H^{4}(X,\mathbb C)_{\mathrm{prim}}\), and their leading Hodge-graded quotient is the degree-\(6\cdot q\) piece of \(S/J(F)\), where \(S=\mathbb C[Z]\) and \(J(F)\) is the Jacobian ideal. This holds for \(0\le q\le 4\). Lower-pole numerators can be multiplied by \(F\) to put all forms over \(F^{q+1}\). The residue and filtration statements, including their projective normalization, are presented in [Diamond, Theorem 2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29157v2#S2).

Let \(\Omega =\iota _\epsilon (dZ_{0}\wedge \cdots \wedge dZ_{5})\), where \(\epsilon =\sum _{i} Z_{i}\partial /\partial Z_{i}\) is the Euler field. Since \(\tau^{*}\Omega =-\Omega \), the Griffiths form

\[
\begin{gathered}
\omega _A = A\cdot \Omega /F^{q+1},       \operatorname{deg} A = 6\cdot q,
\end{gathered}
\]

has invariant residue when \(A\) is \(Y\)-odd. Its residue lies in \(F^{4-q}H^{4}(X,\mathbb C)_{\mathrm{prim}}\). In particular, \(q=1\) presents the invariant (3,1) classes; \(q=2\) presents the invariant Hodge-filtration level \(F^{2}\) and can also contain a contribution of type (3,1). The ambient class is the square of the hyperplane class and is already algebraic. There is no invariant (4,0) part, because \(\Omega \) changes sign. The desired generalized Hodge statement is

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{4}(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau  \subset  N^{1}H^{4}(X,\mathbb Q).
\end{gathered}
\]

Here \(N^{1}\) denotes the rational subspace generated by classes vanishing off divisors. It is a Hodge substructure, by the Gysin description proved in Chapter 3. Solving all \(Y\)-odd targets for \(q=1,2\) puts the invariant \(F^{2}\) part in \(N^{1}\otimes \mathbb C\). Complex conjugation then puts its conjugate there too, and \(F^{2}\) plus its conjugate exhausts the invariant \(H^{4}\). Taking supports for a finite spanning set gives one finite union of divisors supporting everything. Monomials form a convenient input basis, but targets may be arbitrary \(Y\)-odd homogeneous polynomials.

There is no loss in seeking an ambient equation \(D\) for such a support. The Lefschetz theorem on Picard groups gives \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\mathbb Z[\mathcal O_X(1)]\), so an effective divisor has class \(\mathcal O_X(e)\) with \(e>0\). Its section lifts to a homogeneous polynomial \(D\) because \(H^{1}(\mathbb P^{5},\mathcal O(e-6))=0\) in the restriction sequence. The lift is not a multiple of \(F\). A \(\tau \)-stable support can be represented by the even polynomial \(D\cdot \tau (D)\), with repetitions allowed.

## The key equation

For \(v=(v_{0},\ldots ,v_{5})\), set \(v(F)=\sum _{i}v_{i}\partial _{i}F\) and \(\operatorname{div}(v)=\sum _{i}\partial _{i}v_{i}\). A certificate for \((F,q,A)\) is a rational field with homogeneous components of degree \(6\cdot q-5\), with every denominator coprime to \(F\), satisfying

\[
\begin{gathered}
F^{q+1} \mid  K_A(v),       K_A(v) \coloneqq  A - q\cdot v(F) + F\cdot \operatorname{div}(v).
\end{gathered}
\]

Divisibility is in the local ring \(k[Z]_{(F)}\): clear the denominators, which are units there, and check polynomial divisibility. The field can be chosen with \(Y\)-odd components \(v_{0},v_{1},v_{2}\) and \(Y\)-even components \(v_{3},v_{4},v_{5}\). Averaging with respect to \(\tau \) enforces these parities without changing the target.

The bridge to geometry is the rational four-form \(\beta =-\iota _v\Omega /F^q\). Homogeneity makes it a projective form: its weight is zero and contraction with \(\epsilon \) is zero. Its differential satisfies

\[
\begin{gathered}
\omega _A - d\beta  = K_A(v)\cdot\Omega /F^{q+1}.
\end{gathered}
\]

To prove the identity, put \(\mathrm{vol}=dZ_{0}\wedge \cdots \wedge dZ_{5}\). Cartan's formula and \(\operatorname{deg} v_{i}=6\cdot q-5\) give

\[
\begin{gathered}
d(\iota _v\Omega )=\operatorname{div}(v)\cdot\Omega -6\cdot q\iota _{v}\mathrm{vol},\\
dF\wedge \iota _v\Omega =v(F)\cdot\Omega -6\cdot F\iota _{v}\mathrm{vol}.
\end{gathered}
\]

Applying the quotient rule to \(\beta \) cancels the two terms containing \(\iota _{v}\mathrm{vol}\) and yields the displayed formula. The same calculation in \(\mathbb P^{n}\) for \(d=\operatorname{deg} F\) uses \(\operatorname{deg} A=d\cdot(q+1)-(n+1)\) and \(\operatorname{deg} v_{i}=d\cdot q-n\), and replaces \(6\cdot q\) by \(d\cdot q\).

The key equation therefore says that \(\omega _A-d\beta \) has no pole along \(X\). On the complement of the denominator locus, the residue of an exact form and the residue of a form regular across \(X\) both vanish in cohomology, proving sufficiency. The prescribed-support theorem below proves the converse, together with an auxiliary pole bound, without leaving a separate algebraization step implicit. Diamond's Section 2 gives another necessity argument with a bound along \(X\); that bound alone does not impose simple poles along the auxiliary divisor.

## One denominator and the normalized equations

Every finite rational tuple has a common denominator. We may choose it \(Y\)-even, multiplying by its involution conjugate when necessary, and write

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=N/D,       \operatorname{deg} N_{i}=\operatorname{deg}(D)+6\cdot q-5,       \operatorname{gcd}(D,F)=1.
\end{gathered}
\]

A common denominator introduces no restriction on certificate existence. The quotient rule gives

\[
K_A(N/D) = [D\cdot(A\cdot D-q\cdot N(F)) + F\cdot(D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D))]/D^{2}.
\]

For this fixed \(D\), existence is equivalent to the following polynomial system:

\[
\begin{gathered}
E_{1}: q\cdot N(F)=A\cdot D,\\
E_{2}: D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D) \in  (F^q).
\end{gathered}
\]

The forward implication is an Euler normalization, not an extra ansatz. Indeed, the key equation first forces \(A\cdot D-q\cdot N(F)=F\cdot H\) for a polynomial \(H\). Replacing \(N\) by \(N'=N+H\epsilon /(6\cdot q)\) makes \(E_{1}\) exact. Since \(\operatorname{deg} H=\operatorname{deg}(D)+6\cdot q-6\), Euler's identity also gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N')-N'(D) = D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D)+D\cdot H,
\end{gathered}
\]

which is precisely the expression already required to lie in \((F^q)\). Degrees and parities are preserved.

For fixed \(D\), both equations are linear in the coefficients of \(N\). One can compare coefficients after reducing \(E_{2}\) modulo \(F^q\), or introduce a quotient polynomial and impose an exact identity. Thus the unrestricted fixed-denominator question is finite linear algebra. Restricting \(N\) to a convenient smaller space changes that question and requires a separate completeness argument.

A certificate is **strict** when \(K_A(v)=0\) as a rational function. In normalized form this means \(E_{1}\) holds and \(E_{2}\) vanishes identically, rather than merely modulo \(F^q\). Strictness distinguishes individual witnesses. Ordinary and strict certificates have the same existence problem when the denominator is unrestricted, by the normal-form theorem in [§5.3](#technical-information/computation). That conversion may change the support and denominator degree, so the fixed-\(D\) system must retain the full \(E_2\) quotient.

## Euler freedom and denominator gauges

For every homogeneous rational \(\phi \) of degree \(6\cdot q-6\),

\[
\begin{gathered}
q(\phi\cdot\epsilon )(F)=6\cdot q\phi F=F\cdot \operatorname{div}(\phi\cdot\epsilon ).
\end{gathered}
\]

Consequently \(v\) and \(v+\phi\cdot\epsilon \) have the same \(K_A\). An Euler shift preserves strictness as well as ordinary solvability. With \(\phi  Y\)-odd it also preserves parity. The preceding normalization uses \(\phi =H/(6\cdot q\cdot D)\), whose poles remain legal.

There are also formally invisible Euler fields with poles on \(X\), such as \((P/F)\epsilon \) for \(\operatorname{deg} P=6\cdot q\). These are not legal certificate fields: the coprimality requirement forbids their denominator. A coefficient search which admits \(D\) proportional to \(F\) can therefore detect spurious solutions. Homogeneity and small residual alone do not certify legality.

One further gauge is useful for sextic denominators at \(q=1\):

\[
\begin{gathered}
(D,N) \mapsto  (D+t\cdot F, N+t\cdot A\cdot \epsilon /6).
\end{gathered}
\]

It preserves \(E_{1}\) and \(E_{2}\) modulo \(F\), and \(V(F,D+t\cdot F)=V(F,D)\). Coprimality is preserved as well. It need not preserve strictness, since it changes the rational field itself. This gauge is distinct from adding an Euler field to a fixed \(v\).

Indeed, put \(B_D(N)=D\cdot \operatorname{div}(N)-N(D)\). For \(q=1\) and \(\operatorname{deg} D=6\), the shifted numerator has \(N'(F)=A(D+t\cdot F)\). Euler's identity gives \(\operatorname{div}(A\cdot \epsilon /6)=2\cdot A\) and \((A\cdot \epsilon /6)(D)=A\cdot D\). Expanding then gives

\[
B_{D+t\cdot F}(N+t\cdot A\cdot \epsilon /6) = B_D(N)+t\cdot F(\operatorname{div} N+t\cdot A),
\]

using \(E_{1}\) to cancel the remaining terms. This proves precisely the stated modulo-\(F\) invariance.

## Prescribed support and pole multiplicity

The support of a divisor ignores multiplicities; a rational primitive does not. These facts must be kept separate when fixing a denominator.

**Prescribed-support theorem.** Let \(D\) be nonconstant, homogeneous, \(Y\)-even and coprime to \(F\), and let \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\) be a squarefree equation of \(V(D)\). For \(1\le q\le 4\), the following statements are equivalent:

1. \(\operatorname{Res}_X(\omega _A)\) vanishes on \(X\setminus V(D)\).
2. A certificate exists with poles confined to \(V(D)\).
3. A certificate exists with denominator \(D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\).

In particular, \(D^q\) also suffices. Over the field of definition of \(F,A,D\), the numerator can be chosen over that same field. The field can be chosen with the prescribed component parities. With the even presentation \(D^q\), its numerator has those same parities; a squarefree equation \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\) can itself be odd, in which case its numerator transforms accordingly. No smoothness or normal-crossing hypothesis is imposed on \(V(D)\) or its intersection with \(X\). Without a field-parity requirement, the same equivalence applies to arbitrary homogeneous \(D\).

We prove the slightly more general statement for a smooth degree-\(d\) hypersurface \(X\subset P=\mathbb P^{n}\), with \(n\ge 2, 1\le q\le n-1\) and \(\operatorname{deg} A=d\cdot(q+1)-(n+1)\). Put \(R=V(D_{\mathrm{red}}), e=\operatorname{deg} D_{\mathrm{red}}\), and work over \(\mathbb C\) until the final linear descent. We use unshifted de Rham complexes, with differential forms in degrees \(0,\ldots ,n\).

The external inputs are the following standard facts about mixed Hodge modules and projective space. They are stated here to specify exactly what the proof uses.

- Localization along a reduced divisor \(T\) carries a Hodge filtration \(\mathcal F\) with \(\mathcal F_{-1}\mathcal O_P(*T)=0\) and \(\mathcal F_{k}\mathcal O_P(*T)\subset \mathcal O_P((k+1)T)\) for \(k\ge 0\); equality holds when \(T\) is smooth. Inclusions and quotients of these filtered modules are strict. See [Mustaţă–Popa, Hodge ideals, equation (0.1) and §§4–7](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~mpopa/papers/SI.pdf).
- Projective direct image is strict: for a filtered mixed Hodge module \(M\) on projective \(P\), the map from the hypercohomology of \(\mathcal F^p\operatorname{DR}(M)\) to that of \(\operatorname{DR}(M)\) is injective. Here its \(j\)-th term is \(\Omega ^{j}_P\otimes \mathcal F_{j-p}M\). See [Mustaţă–Popa, Hodge ideals for \(\mathbb Q\)-divisors, §1 and equation (1.1)](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/jep.94.pdf).
- Algebraic de Rham comparison identifies localization with the derived direct image from the divisor complement; this is the comparison input used in [Diamond, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29157v2#S2.SS3). Bott vanishing gives \(H^{i}(P,\Omega ^{j}_P(b))=0\) for \(b>0\) and \(i>0\), as recalled in [Hodge ideals, §25](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~mpopa/papers/SI.pdf); line bundles on \(\mathbb P^{n}\) also have zero \(H^{1}\) for \(n\ge 2\).

**Proof.** Set

\[
\begin{gathered}
M=\mathcal O_P(*(X+R))/\mathcal O_P(*R).
\end{gathered}
\]

The residue comparison is \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,\operatorname{DR}(M))\cong H^{n-1}(X\setminus R,\mathbb C)\), with the usual residue Tate shift. To see the shift, work first on \(P\setminus R\) with a local normal coordinate \(t\) for the smooth \(X\). Modulo regular forms, all higher normal poles are exact and the only normal de Rham class is \(\mathrm dt/t\), one degree higher than the corresponding class on \(X\). Localization along \(R\) extends this residue identification to \(P\). Since \(X\) is smooth, \(\omega _A\) belongs to the top term of \(\mathcal F^{n-q}\operatorname{DR}(M)\): it comes from \(\mathcal F_q\mathcal O_P(*X)=\mathcal O_P((q+1)X)\). If its residue vanishes, strictness of projective direct image says that its class already vanishes in \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,\mathcal F^{n-q}\operatorname{DR}(M))\). This is the only step that requires more than unfiltered de Rham exactness.

For \(n-q\le j\le n\) put \(a_j=j-n+q+1\) and introduce the finite complex

\[
\begin{gathered}
K^{j}=\Omega ^{j}_P\otimes [\mathcal O_P(a_j(X+R))/\mathcal O_P(a_jR)],\\
K^{j}=0 \;\text{for}\; j<n-q.
\end{gathered}
\]

Differentiation increases each pole order by at most one, so it gives the differential of \(K^{\bullet} \). The Hodge pole bound provides a map of complexes \(\mathcal F^{n-q}\operatorname{DR}(M)\to K^{\bullet} \). To check this on quotients, a filtered representative has poles at most \(a_j\) along both \(X\) and \(R\). A representative lying in \(\mathcal O_P(*R)\) therefore lies in \(\mathcal O_P(a_jR)\). Strictness identifies precisely those representatives with \(\mathcal F_{a_j-1}\mathcal O_P(*R)\), so the quotient map is well defined. Consequently the class of \(\omega _A\) is zero in \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,K^{\bullet} )\).

Each \(K^{j}\) has zero higher cohomology. Indeed, in

\[
\begin{gathered}
0 \to  \Omega ^{j}_P(a_jR) \to  \Omega ^{j}_P(a_j(X+R)) \to  K^{j} \to  0
\end{gathered}
\]

both twists are positive because \(a_j\ge 1\) and \(e>0\). Bott vanishing and the long exact sequence give the claim. Hence \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,K^{\bullet} )\) is computed by global sections. The zero class of the top section \(\omega _A\) supplies a global section \(\overline{\beta }\) of \(K^{n-1}\) with \(d\overline{\beta }=\omega _A\). The same sequence in degree \(n-1\), and \(H^{1}(P,\Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot R))=0\), lift it to

\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta  \in  H^{0}(P,\Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot X+q\cdot R)).
\end{gathered}
\]

Thus \(\omega _A-d\beta \) has poles only on \(R\). In particular, the primitive has at most \(q\)-fold poles along every component of \(R\) and along \(X\), with no added support.

It remains to obtain the vector field, rather than merely assert that a rational form can be represented. The identity \(\Omega ^{n-1}_P\cong T_P(-n-1)\) and the twisted Euler sequence give

\[
0 \to  \mathcal O_P(q(d+e)-n-1) \to  \mathcal O_P(q(d+e)-n)^{n+1} \to  \Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot X+q\cdot R) \to  0.
\]

The left term has zero \(H^{1}\). Therefore \(\beta \) is represented by a homogeneous polynomial tuple \(N\) of degree \(q(d+e)-n\):

\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta =-\iota _N\Omega /(F^q\cdot D_{\mathrm{red}}^q).
\end{gathered}
\]

With \(v=N/D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\), the differential identity proved above converts the absence of an \(X\)-pole into the key equation. This proves \(1\Longrightarrow 3\). The implication \(3\Longrightarrow 2\) is immediate, and \(2\Longrightarrow 1\) is the residue argument already given. Multiplying \(N\) by \((D/D_{\mathrm{red}})^q\) gives the prescribed denominator \(D^q\). Averaging the field under \(\tau \) preserves this even denominator and the target, and enforces the component parities. It can also retain \(D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\), since stability of its reduced support implies \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\circ \tau =\pm D_{\mathrm{red}}\). Finally, the fixed-denominator normalized equations form a finite linear system over the original coefficient field. Consistency over \(\mathbb C\) implies consistency over that field by Gaussian elimination. ∎

This also proves the claimed necessity of certificates for an arbitrary divisor support: choose an ambient \(D\) cutting that divisor, apply the theorem, and use the resulting polynomial tuple. If the original coefficients lie in a smaller field, the descent argument below gives a certificate over that field, possibly with a different support. The proof bounds poles on a chosen support; it supplies no bound on the degree \(e\) of the support itself.

At **\(q=1\)**, therefore, existence over \(D\) is equivalent to existence over any \(D^{m}\). An exact failure of the full fixed-\(D\) linear system excludes every higher power of that \(D\). At **\(q=2\)**, the definitive test on its support uses \(D^{2}\). Failure over \(D\) alone need not exclude support.

The distinction is sharp. Set

\[
\begin{gathered}
D=X_{0}^{6}+X_{1}^{6}+X_{2}^{6},       E=Y_{0}^{6}+Y_{1}^{6}+Y_{2}^{6},       F=D+E,\\
A=X_{0}^{3}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{3}\cdot Y_{0}\cdot Y_{1}\cdot Y_{2},       q=2.
\end{gathered}
\]

Writing \(\epsilon _X\) and \(\epsilon _Y\) for the two block Euler fields, the strict certificate is

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=A(F\epsilon _X-D\cdot \epsilon _Y)/(12\cdot D^{2}).
\end{gathered}
\]

For the numerator \(N_{2}=A(F\epsilon _X-D\cdot \epsilon _Y)/12\), direct blockwise differentiation gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
2\cdot N_{2}(F)=A\cdot D^{2},       \operatorname{div} N_{2}=A\cdot F,       N_{2}(D^{2})=A\cdot F\cdot D^{2}.
\end{gathered}
\]

These identities prove both normalized equations, with \(E_{2}\) identically zero. The field has degree seven and the required parities. Fermat smoothness is immediate from its partial derivatives, and \(D\) is coprime to \(F\) because \(D\) and \(E\) involve disjoint variables and have no common factor.

There is no numerator over \(D\). To prove this without an ansatz, normalize \(E_{1}\) and average a hypothetical numerator over the six independent sixth-root coordinate scalings, projecting onto the character of \(A\). Both \(F\) and \(D\) are invariant, so this operation preserves the fixed denominator and the two equations. The retained monomials in \(N_{i}\) have exponent vector congruent modulo six to \((3,3,3,1,1,1)+e_{i}\). These six residues are all less than six and already sum to the required numerator degree thirteen. Thus \(N_{i}=c_{i}AZ_{i}\) is the entire surviving space, not a selected family. \(E_{1}\) forces \(c_{0}=c_{1}=c_{2}=1/12\) and \(c_{3}=c_{4}=c_{5}=0\). For this numerator, \(\operatorname{div} N=A\) and \(N(D)=A\cdot D/2\), so \(E_{2}\) is \(A\cdot D/2\). It is not divisible even by \(F\). This excludes every original numerator because normalization and averaging preserve existence.

These bounds leave the central search problem untouched: they do not bound the degree of the reduced support that must be found.

## Combining certificates and descending coefficients

For fixed \(F\) and \(q\), the equation is linear in the pair \((A,v)\). If \(v_j\) serves \(A_j\), then \(\sum _{j}c_j\cdot v_j\) serves \(\sum _{j}c_jA_j\). A product of the denominators supplies a common denominator, so supported target spaces add when supports are united. A decomposition into symmetry characters can therefore organize a search without requiring one denominator to serve every component separately.

In cleared form, certificates \((D,N,Q)\) for \(A\) and \((E,M,R)\) for \(B\) combine as

\[
D_{A+B}=DE,\qquad N_{A+B}=EN+DM,\qquad
Q_{A+B}=E^2Q+D^2R.
\]

The resulting defect is \(E^2\mathcal E_A+D^2\mathcal E_B=F^{q+1}(E^2Q+D^2R)\). Nonzero quotient terms therefore cause no obstruction to addition. Denominator legality is preserved by products, and for positive \(q\) each numerator has degree \(\deg D+\deg E+6q-5\).

If \(F\) and \(A\) are rational and \(v\) is defined over a number field \(K\), normalized trace gives a rational certificate:

\[
\begin{gathered}
v_\mathbb Q = \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(v)/[K:\mathbb Q].
\end{gathered}
\]

To prove descent, sum the conjugate fields over all embeddings of \(K\) into a normal closure. Differentiation commutes with each embedding, so each conjugate serves the same \(A\). Their average is Galois-invariant and hence rational. The product of the conjugate denominators is the norm, clears that average, and has degree \([K:\mathbb Q]\operatorname{deg} D\) before cancellation. Each factor is coprime to \(F\), so the norm remains legal. Homogeneity and parity are unchanged.

The same argument works for every finite extension \(K/k\) in characteristic zero. It also suffices to descend an initially complex certificate for data over \(k\). Fix its denominator degree and write the normalized equations in the finitely many coefficients of \(D,N\) and the \(E_{2}\) quotient. These are polynomial equations over \(k\). Legality is an open condition: at least one coefficient of the remainder of \(D\) modulo \(F\) is nonzero. Choose such a coefficient and invert it using one additional variable. A complex point of this finite polynomial system implies a point over an algebraic closure of \(k\), by the Nullstellensatz; its finitely many coordinates generate a finite extension. Trace then gives a certificate over \(k\). This proves descent of existence, without claiming to preserve an initially transcendental supporting equation.

For a bundled target \(A+cB\), with \(1,c\) linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the nondegenerate trace pairing supplies \(p\in K\) satisfying \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p\cdot c)=0\). Indeed, evaluation of that pairing on the independent vectors \(1,c\) defines a surjective linear map \(K\to \mathbb Q^{2}\). Applying trace to the certificate identity for \(p\cdot v\) shows that \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p\cdot v)\) serves \(A\). More generally a trace-dual basis extracts every rational component of an extension-field target. Trace over passive function fields appears in Chapter 2, where commutation with the relevant derivatives is proved for that setting.

For completeness, character averaging also has an explicit formula. Suppose a finite diagonal group acts by \(\gamma :Z_{i}\mapsto \gamma _{i}Z_{i}\), with \(F\circ \gamma =\mu _\gamma F\) and \(A\circ \gamma =\nu _\gamma A\). Define

\[
\begin{gathered}
(T_\gamma v)_{i}=\mu _\gamma (v_{i}\circ \gamma )/(\nu _\gamma \gamma _{i}).
\end{gathered}
\]

The chain rule gives \(K_A(T_\gamma v)=K_A(v)\circ \gamma /\nu _\gamma \). Thus averaging \(T_\gamma v\) preserves the certificate and projects onto the required character. A common denominator is the product of the conjugates, so its degree may grow by the group order. This does not justify imposing a single character on \(D\) at a previously chosen degree.

There is a useful exponent description when \(F\) contains all six pure sixth powers. Let \(L(F)\) be the lattice generated by differences of exponents in the support of \(F\). Diagonal substitutions preserving \(F\) up to scalar are exactly the characters of \(\mathbb Z^{6}/L(F)\). Modulo global scalar substitutions this is a finite group: the six pure powers force all \(\gamma _{i}^{6}\) to agree, and a common scalar makes them all one. Characters separate its exponent cosets at fixed degree. For a character field component, reduced numerator and denominator are both eigenvectors: the identity obtained by transforming their coprime quotient forces each factor to be carried to a scalar multiple of itself. Their characters differ by that of \(A\) times the \(i\)-th coordinate divided by the character of \(F\). This proves the support-coset rule without discarding rational fields, though averaging may increase degree.

For a full-support \(Y\)-even sextic, \(L(F)\) is exactly the lattice of vectors of total sum zero and even \(Y\)-sum. One inclusion follows from parity. Conversely, exponent differences realize all within-\(X\) and within-\(Y\) coordinate transfers, and also \(2(e_{X_{i}}-e_{Y_{j}})\); these generate that lattice. Hence all \(Y\)-odd targets of one degree belong to a single coset. Fine target-character decompositions are a property of structured \(F\), not an available simplification for general \(F\).

## Jacobian reduction and exact verification

Let \(J(F)=(\partial _{0}F,\ldots ,\partial _{5}F)\). If \(A=\sum _{i}G_{i}\partial _{i}F\), taking \(v=G/q\) gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
K_A(G/q)=F\cdot \operatorname{div}(G)/q.
\end{gathered}
\]

This lowers the pole order by one: modulo an exact form, \(\omega _A\) becomes \((\operatorname{div} G/q)\Omega /F^q\). Membership in \(J(F)\) therefore kills the leading Hodge-graded piece; it need not kill the whole residue class. For invariant \(q=1\) targets it does kill the class: the lower contribution would lie in the anti-invariant (4,0) space. Equivalently, after parity averaging, \(\operatorname{div}(G)\) is a \(Y\)-odd constant and hence zero.

For a concrete \(q=2\) example in our diagonal involution coordinates, take Fermat \(F\) and

\[
\begin{gathered}
A=6\cdot X_{0}^{6}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0},       G_{0}=X_{0}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0},       G_{i}=0 \;\text{for}\; i>0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Then \(A=\sum G_{i}\partial _{i}F\) is \(Y\)-odd and belongs to \(J(F)\), but one reduction gives the \(q=1\) numerator \(X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0}/2\). All of its exponents are at most four, so it is nonzero in the Fermat Jacobian ring \(\mathbb C[Z]/(Z_{0}^{5},\ldots ,Z_{5}^{5})\). Griffiths's graded isomorphism makes its (3,1) class nonzero. Thus the original \(q=2\) residue is nonzero, despite Jacobian membership. A complete reduction algorithm must retain this lower-pole target.

For an explicit field, clearing denominators reduces verification to polynomial identities and the homogeneity and coprimality conditions. A nonzero remainder divisible by \(F^{q+1}\) is valid. [Chapter 5](#technical-information/computation) gives the complete polynomial criterion and proves equivalence with strict existence when the denominator may change.

# 3. Geometric support, finite groups and surface fibrations

[Previous: binary sextics and torsion contacts](#technical-information/binary-blocks) · [Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: split sextics and K3 correspondences](#technical-information/split-and-k3)

A certificate constructs a primitive on the complement of a divisor. Geometry establishes the same vanishing through Gysin maps and correspondences. This chapter develops the shared tools: finite quotients, correspondences over a common base, covering rational curves, surface fibrations with \(p_g=q=0\), and supported projectors in families. The reflection and relative-projector results supply the two parts of [Chapter 3B](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds). Fano support and correspondence transfer also underlie the quadratic-net theorem of [Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets). Work in characteristic zero; cohomology is rational, or algebraic de Rham after scalar extension.

## 3.1 Divisor support and its source

For a smooth projective variety \(X\), a class is divisor-supported if it vanishes on \(X\setminus Z\) for some divisor \(Z\). The resulting subspace is \(N^{1}H^{k}(X)\). Here is the Gysin description of that space. Take an embedded resolution \(r:\widetilde{X}\to X\) whose reduced inverse image \(E=\bigcup E_i\) is a simple normal-crossing divisor. Localization places \(r^{*}\alpha \) in the image of \(H^{k}_E(\widetilde{X})\to H^{k}(\widetilde{X})\). The Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence for supports and purity give, for an intersection of \(c\) components, the terms \(H^{k-c-1}(E_{i_{1}}\cap \cdots \cap E_{i_c})(-c)\) contributing to degree \(k\). Their weights are \(k+c-1\). The \(c=1\) terms have weight \(k\), while all deeper intersections have larger weight. Strictness of mixed-Hodge morphisms therefore makes the image in the pure \(H^{k}(\widetilde{X})\) equal to the image of \(\sum _i H^{k-2}(E_i)(-1)\). Push forward and use \(r_*r^{*}=\operatorname{id}\). This proves that \(N^{1}H^{k}(X)\) is generated by the resulting proper Gysin images from smooth divisors. The localization, purity and strictness inputs are stated in [Chapter 1](#technical-information/certificates).

On a fourfold the (3,1) part must consequently come from \(H^{2,0}(E_i)\). Components contracted into codimension at least two have zero (3,1) image: degree-four classes supported in codimension two come from degree-zero classes of surfaces with twist \((-2)\), and hence have type (2,2). Thus resolutions of the actual divisor components supply the relevant holomorphic two-forms. A count of singularities or contact multiplicities does not determine their Gysin map.

On a smooth sextic fourfold this forces singularities on any divisor supporting a nonzero (3,1) class. Lefschetz gives \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\mathbb Z[\mathcal O_X(1)]\), so every nonzero effective divisor \(D\) is ample. The sequence \(0\to\mathcal O_X(-D)\to\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_D\to0\), the vanishing \(H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0\), and Kodaira vanishing with Serre duality give \(H^2(D,\mathcal O_D)=0\). If \(D\) is normal with rational singularities, a resolution \(\widetilde D\to D\) has the same coherent cohomology, hence \(H^{2,0}(\widetilde D)=0\). Such a component has zero (3,1) Gysin image. Therefore a support for a nonzero (3,1) class must contain a component which is nonnormal or has nonrational singularities. In particular, replacing a support by a smooth divisor need not preserve its cohomological role.

Support is stable under finite sums: take the union of the supports. For a dominant generically finite proper morphism between smooth varieties of the same dimension, pullback and pushforward preserve divisor support. Pullback uses the inverse image of a support; pushforward uses its proper image, which still has codimension at least one. The degree identity \(p_*p^{*}=\operatorname{deg}(p) \operatorname{id}\) follows from the projection formula.

If a finite group \(G\) acts on a variety \(M\), rational cohomology of the quotient is the invariant cohomology. One proof uses the finite quotient map \(\pi \): the invariant part of \(\pi _*\mathbb Q\) is the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q\), higher direct images vanish, and taking \(G\)-invariants is exact over \(\mathbb Q\). When \(M\) and the quotient are smooth, the corresponding identities are

\[
\begin{gathered}
\pi _*\pi^{*} = |G| \operatorname{id},             \pi^{*}\pi _* = \sum _{g\in G} g^{*}.
\end{gathered}
\]

They also hold for branched quotients: the top-dimensional cycle of \(M\times _{M/G}M\) is the sum of the graphs of the group elements. Their intersections over the branch locus do not add a top-dimensional component.

**Quotient-transfer lemma.** Let \(M\) be smooth projective with a faithful finite \(G\)-action, and let \(N\) be a smooth projective model of \(M/G\). Then \(H^{k}(N)\) is divisor-supported if and only if \(H^{k}(M)^G\) is divisor-supported.

**Proof.** Resolve the quotient rational map equivariantly as \(r:R\to M\) and \(p:R\to N\). Here \(r\) is a sequence of blowups with smooth centers and \(p\) is generically finite of degree \(|G|\). The blowup decomposition

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{k}(\operatorname{Bl}_C M) = H^{k}(M) \oplus  \bigoplus _{j=1}^{\operatorname{codim} C-1} H^{k-2\cdot j}(C)(-j)
\end{gathered}
\]

shows that \(\operatorname{ker} r_*\) is supported on the exceptional divisors. For this formula, write the exceptional divisor as \(E=\mathbb P(N_{C/M})\) and \(\xi =c_{1}(\mathcal O_E(1))\). The added summands map by \(\gamma \mapsto i_*(\xi ^{j-1}\pi^{*}\gamma )\). The projective-bundle decomposition of \(H^{*}(E)\), together with the localization comparison across \(\operatorname{Bl}_C M\setminus E\cong M\setminus C\), gives the displayed decomposition; \(r_*r^{*}=\operatorname{id}\) splits off \(H^{k}(M)\). If \(H^{k}(M)^G\) is supported, then \(r_*p^{*}\beta \) is supported for every \(\beta \in H^{k}(N)\). Hence \(r^{*}r_*p^{*}\beta \) is supported, and \(p^{*}\beta \) differs from it by an exceptional class. Push forward and divide by \(|G|\) to support \(\beta \).

Conversely, take \(\alpha \in H^{k}(M)^G\) and assume \(H^{k}(N)\) is supported. The class \(p^{*}p_*r^{*}\alpha \) is supported. Over the dense open where \(p\) is the finite group quotient, transfer identifies it with \(\sum _g g^{*}r^{*}\alpha =|G|r^{*}\alpha \). Their difference is supported on the omitted boundary, which can be included in a divisor. Push forward by \(r\) and divide by \(|G|\). This proves the lemma and explains why the boundary cannot be dropped. The same proof shows invariance of the all-supported assertion under smooth projective birational modification. ∎

These constructions use algebraic graphs, blowups and traces. An abstract Hodge isomorphism alone would not transport a supporting equation.

### Correspondences over a common base

Let \(M,N\) be smooth projective varieties of the same dimension \(d\). A \(d\)-cycle \(C\subset M\times N\) whose components dominate both factors preserves divisor support:
\[
C_*\bigl(N^1H^k(M)\bigr)\subseteq N^1H^k(N).
\]
Resolve each component of \(C\). Both projections are proper and generically finite. The inverse image of a supporting divisor has dimension at most \(d-1\), and its proper image has dimension at most \(d-1\) as well. Pullback and pushforward through this resolution give the asserted correspondence action. The same argument applies componentwise when \(N\) is disconnected.

**Common-base boundary lemma.** Suppose smooth projective \(d\)-folds \(M_i\) have dominant morphisms to one projective variety \(B\), and all correspondences under consideration lie in the relative products \(M_i\times_B M_j\). Let \(B^\circ\subset B\) be dense open and \(M_i^\circ=M_i\times_B B^\circ\). An identity between the restricted correspondences, or their composites, gives the same identity on global cohomology modulo classes supported on the complement of the output open.

Indeed, if the output point lies over \(B^\circ\), the relative-product condition forces every intermediate point and the input point to lie over \(B^\circ\). Restriction therefore commutes with each proper correspondence action and with its composites. The error operator has image in
\[
\ker\bigl(H^k(M_j)\longrightarrow H^k(M_j^\circ)\bigr).
\]
The complement is a proper closed subset and can be included in a divisor. This proves the claim. The common base is essential to this argument: equality on an arbitrary product open alone does not control contributions from the omitted source.

### Averaging projectors and the part served by a quotient

Let a finite group \(G\) act on a smooth projective variety \(M\), and write
\[
e_K=\frac1{|K|}\sum_{k\in K}k\in\mathbb Q[G]
\]
for a subgroup \(K\). Use \(g\mapsto(g^{-1})^*\) for the left action on cohomology; averaging has the same image under either pullback convention. Suppose smooth projective models of \(M/K_1,\ldots,M/K_s\) have divisor-supported \(H^m\). Form the two-sided ideal
\[
I=\sum_j\mathbb Q[G]e_{K_j}\mathbb Q[G].
\]
Then
\[
I H^m(M)\subseteq N^1H^m(M).
\]
Indeed, quotient transfer supports \(e_{K_j}H^m(M)=H^m(M)^{K_j}\), and \(N^1\) is stable under every group element and under finite sums. This proves the assertion for each product \(a e_{K_j}b\) and hence for \(I\).

Maschke's theorem makes the scope exact at the representation-theoretic level. A simple rational representation \(\rho\) occurs in the ideal \(I\) precisely when \(\rho^{K_j}\ne0\) for at least one \(j\): in its simple algebra factor, \(e_{K_j}\) is nonzero exactly under that condition, and any nonzero element generates the factor as a two-sided ideal. Thus the supported invariant spaces, together with their \(G\)-translates, serve the entire isotypic component of every such \(\rho\). Any projector lying in \(I\) has supported image. This is a criterion for these quotients, not an assertion that the remaining representations lack support from other correspondences.

The same argument applies on a finite auxiliary cover. Resolve a projective model equivariantly, compute the ideal there, and use the proper generically finite map to the original variety. A physical class is served when its pullback lies in the supported image; normalized pushforward then descends the support. Reflections, deck traces and exchanges are instances of this one procedure. Finding more curves on a fixed quotient improves its construction, but cannot add a representation absent from its averaging projector.

### Descent through a deck action and an exchange

Quotients of an auxiliary cover can support complementary parts of the original variety's cohomology. The following criterion isolates the relations needed for their combined descent.

**Proposition.** Let \(p:Z\to X\) be a proper dominant generically finite morphism of smooth complex projective varieties. Let \(d,g\) be finite-order automorphisms of \(Z,X\), respectively; let \(r,\sigma\) be commuting involutions of \(Z\), and \(\tau\) an involution of \(X\). Put \(e=\sigma d\sigma\), and suppose
\[
pd=p,\qquad pe=gp,\qquad pr=\tau p.
\]
If smooth projective models of \(Z/\langle r,\sigma\rangle\) and \(X/\langle g\rangle\) have divisor-supported \(H^k\), then
\[
H^k(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau\subseteq N^1H^k(X,\mathbb Q).
\]

**Proof.** Quotient transfer in §3.1 supports the corresponding invariant spaces. Take \(\xi\in H^k(X)^\tau\), and write \(a=p^*\xi\) in
\[
V=H^k(Z)/N^1H^k(Z).
\]
Then \(d^*a=r^*a=a\). Since \(r,\sigma\) commute, \(p^*\xi+\sigma^*p^*\xi\) is invariant under both; its image \(a+\sigma^*a\) is therefore zero in \(V\). Thus \(\sigma^*a=-a\), which gives
\[
e^*a=\sigma^*d^*\sigma^*a=a.
\]
Let \(\operatorname{Av}_h\) denote averaging over a finite cyclic action. The relation \(pe=gp\) and dominance of \(p\) imply that the order of \(g\) divides that of \(e\), so
\[
a=\operatorname{Av}_e a=p^*(\operatorname{Av}_g\xi)=0
\quad\text{in }V.
\]
The last equality follows from support of \(H^k(X)^{\langle g\rangle}\). Finally, proper pushforward preserves divisor support and \(p_*p^*\xi=\deg(p)\xi\). This proves the claim. ∎

For a rational presentation, apply the criterion after exhibiting a finite symmetry group and resolving its action together with the cover projection equivariantly. Finiteness is a hypothesis to check; individual birational symmetries do not by themselves supply the required models.

## 3.2 Curve and surface fibrations

The two criteria below reduce cohomology over an affine base to classes which vanish off a divisor. Rational curves give vanishing directly. Surface fibers with \(p_g=q=0\) give it after removing finitely many relative divisor classes. Finite trace descends the resulting support in both cases.

### Covering rational curves

**Support theorem.** Let \(W\) be a smooth projective \(n\)-fold, \(n>0\). Suppose an actual morphism \(e:\mathbb P^{1}\times S\to W\) is dominant and generically finite, where \(S\) is smooth integral affine of dimension \(n-1\). Then all \(H^{n}(W)\) is supported on one divisor.

**Proof.** Put \(V=\mathbb A^{1}\times S\). Homotopy invariance and affine de Rham computation give

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{n}_{\mathrm{dR}}(V)=H^{n}_{\mathrm{dR}}(S)=0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Indeed, on \(S\) the de Rham complex is a complex of global sections ending in degree \(n-1\). Compactify \(\mathbb P^{1}\times S\) projectively and take the closure \(\Gamma \) of the graph of \(e\). Its projection \(p:\Gamma \to W\) is proper and generically finite, and \(\Gamma \) contains \(V\) as an open subset. The boundary \(\Gamma \setminus V\) has dimension at most \(n-1\), so its proper image is a proper closed subset of \(W\).

Remove this image and the positive-dimensional-fiber locus of \(p\). On the remaining open the map is finite. Remove its non-étale locus as well; characteristic zero makes this another proper closed subset. Enlarge the union of the removed sets to a divisor \(E\). Then \(p^{-1}(W\setminus E)\) lies in \(V\) and is finite étale of positive degree \(m\) over \(W\setminus E\). The pullback of each global \(\alpha \in H^{n}(W)\) vanishes on \(V\), hence on this smaller open. Finite étale trace gives \(m\alpha |_{W\setminus E}=0\). Notice that no vanishing of all \(H^{n}(p^{-1}(W\setminus E))\) is asserted or needed. ∎

### Fano varieties

A smooth Fano variety is covered by rational curves. The same holds for a normal projective variety with ample \(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier anticanonical divisor; the covering curves may pass through its singular locus. These are consequences of the bend-and-break theorems in [Debarre, Theorems 7.5 and 7.7, Proposition 9.12 and Corollary 9.13](https://perso.imj-prg.fr/wp-content/uploads/debarre-pub/M22.pdf).

For Kawamata log terminal (klt) singularities, [Zhang, Proposition 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0408301) gives a stronger sufficient condition: if \(-K_W\) is nef and big, every smooth projective model of \(W\) is uniruled.
