Here \(d_\Lambda\) differentiates coefficients while holding the ambient coordinates fixed. The degree is \(6+3=9\), as required.

For completeness, on the cover \(g_1\ne0, g_2\ne0\), lifts of \(R|_C\) through (3B.3.1) are \((R/g_1,0,0)\) and \((0,R/g_2,0)\). Their difference represents the obstruction. If \(v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)\), then \(g_1v_1+g_2v_2+kv_3=0\), and its Serre pairing is represented by

\[
\frac{Rv_3}{g_1g_2}\,\theta_C,
\qquad
\theta_C=\operatorname{Res}_C\frac{\Omega_{\mathbb P}}{f_1f_2h}.
\]

The adjunction form \(\theta_C\) has twist \(K_C\otimes\mathcal O_C(-1)\), canceled by the degree-one coefficient. Its Serre trace is exactly the residue above; the actual velocity has \(v_3=-D(h)\). This proves (3B.3.4), including a constant normalization rather than an unspecified function of the parameter.

If \(f_1=\lambda u+q\), eliminating \(u\) contributes \(1/\lambda\) to the four-variable residue. One differentiates \(h\) first and then substitutes \(u=-q/\lambda\); differentiating the already substituted cubic gives a different expression. At nonreduced intersections the Artinian residue remains valid without division by a pointwise Jacobian.

On \(\Lambda\), these forms extend holomorphically because they equal \(\Gamma^*H^{2,1}(T)^-\). They are therefore closed. Once the pullback is injective, the polarization argument in §3B.6 makes \(\Gamma_*\Gamma^*\) invertible on the negative sector. Thus these canonical forms suffice to recover every source after applying that inverse. The identity \(\Gamma_*\eta_R=R\) does not follow without this inversion; the moving-point trace formula still requires its exact differential correction.

## 3B.4 A finite spanning criterion and an exact witness

### The criterion

Weighted residues give

\[
H^{2,1}(T)^-\simeq R_6(G)^-,\qquad \dim R_6(G)^-=48.
\]

For example, at the weighted Fermat equation the ring is
\(\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,u]/(a^5,b^5,c^5,d^5,u^2)\); its negative degree-six monomials have dimensions 32 without \(u\) and 16 with \(u\). The dimensions are constant throughout the smooth invariant family.

Suppose a nonconstant algebraic family of curves on a fixed \(T\) has smooth general member, \(h^0N=h^1N=1\), and a nonzero formal obstruction functional

\[
\ell(t)\in\bigl(R_6(G)^-\bigr)^\vee((t)).
\]

By (3B.3.3), this functional differs from the actual correspondence differential by a common nonzero meromorphic scalar. If its coefficient rows span the 48-dimensional dual, then

\[
\Gamma^*:H^{2,1}(T)^-\hookrightarrow H^{1,0}(\Lambda).
\qquad\text{(3B.4.1)}
\]

Indeed, a constant class in the kernel is killed by every coefficient row. Conjugation and Poincaré duality then give

\[
\Gamma_*:H^1(\Lambda)(-1)\twoheadrightarrow H^3(T)^-.
\qquad\text{(3B.4.2)}
\]

In particular \(g(\Lambda)\ge48\). It is the genus of the parameter curve, not the genus four of its fibers, that appears in this inequality. A nodal member is allowed at \(t=0\); the pairing is applied on the smooth punctured branch.

### An integral norm presentation

The following witness makes the criterion effective without a genericity assumption on the chosen coefficients. Set

\[
\begin{gathered}
\kappa=50,\qquad Q=61c^2+110cd+85d^2,\\
B=50c^3+75c^2d+40cd^2+22d^3,\\
f_1=u+Q,\qquad f_2=ab,\qquad g_1=u^2-uQ+Q^2,\\
g_2=\kappa a^4+2\kappa b^4-2a^2b^2
       +\kappa cd(a^2+2c^2),\qquad A=a^3+b^3,
\end{gathered}
\]

and **define** \(G=\Phi(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2,A,B)\). Modulo five this is

\[
G\equiv u^3+a^6+b^6+c^6+d^6.
\]

Its derivatives have no common nonzero zero, proving smoothness in characteristic zero by properness of the singular locus. Modulo 23, the binary forms become

\[
Q=15c^2+18cd+16d^2,\qquad
B=4c^3+6c^2d+17cd^2+22d^3.
\]

Here \(B\) is squarefree and coprime to \(Q\); the nonzero discriminant and resultant give these properties in characteristic zero as well. The curve \(C_0=(f_1,f_2,A+B)\) is the union of the plane cubics

\[
E_a:\ a=0,\ u=-Q,\ b^3+B=0,
\qquad
E_b:\ b=0,\ u=-Q,\ a^3+B=0.
\]

They are smooth and meet transversely at the three roots of \(B\). At those nodes \(g_1=3Q^2\ne0\).

The exact verifier `scripts/verify-norm-contact-span.py`, in the repository’s [reproduction scripts](https://github.com/hodge-computer/sextics/tree/main/scripts), reconstructs the coefficient matrices, kernel directions and Taylor coefficients from this integral presentation; it reads no witness data. It uses lexicographically ordered weighted monomials and exact arithmetic in \(\mathbb F_{23}\) and \(\mathbb F_{23}[v]/(v^2-15)\). Run it with Python and NumPy:

```sh
python3 scripts/verify-norm-contact-span.py
```

The necessary finite results are as follows.

| Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| \(d\Phi\) at the nodal presentation | rank 69; a 69-minor is 10 modulo 23 |
| 69 coordinate directions, two essential kernel directions, and 19 presentation directions | rank 90; determinant 13 modulo 23 |
| Quadratic obstruction on the two-dimensional slice | \(q(s,t)=10s^2+12st+13t^2\), discriminant 15 |
| First-order smoothing forms at the three nodes | \(K_1=9c^2, K_2=15c^2+13cd+18d^2\) |
| Common-root test | \(\gcd(B,q(K_2,-K_1))=1\) |
| Negative degree-six ideal at the nodal presentation | rank 58 |
| First 48 obstruction coefficient rows on one branch | rank 48; minor \(22+2v\), norm 10 |

The two central ranks require characteristic-zero upper bounds, since a modular rank alone supplies only a lower bound. For \(I=(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2,A,B)\), eliminating \(u\) and setting \(a=0\) gives the quotient

\[
\mathbb C[b,c,d]/(b^3,B,Q^2,c^3d).
\]

Its positive degree-six part contains
\(b^2\bigl(\mathbb C[c,d]_4/\langle cB,dB,Q^2,c^3d\rangle\bigr)\), which is nonzero: there are five monomials and at most four relations. Thus \(\operatorname{rank}d\Phi\le69\), and the displayed minor proves equality.

For the negative rank, before the last relation the quotient is \(U\otimes V\), with

\[
U=\mathbb C[a,b]/(ab,a^3+b^3),\qquad
V=\mathbb C[c,d]/(B,Q^2).
\]

Its negative degree-six piece is \(aV_5\oplus bV_5\oplus a^3V_3\), of dimension \(1+1+3=5\). The remaining generator \(cd(a^2+2c^2)\), multiplied by \(ac,ad,bc,bd\), imposes at most three relations: the last two lie in the same one-dimensional \(bV_5\). Hence the negative quotient has dimension at least two; the 58-minor again gives equality.

### Lifting the branch and its span

Construct the characteristic-zero kernel vectors by fixing the same free coordinates in Gaussian elimination and solving with the 69-minor. The exact rank bound makes the remaining row dependent, so these are genuine tangent vectors whose reductions are the computed ones; the modular vectors are not treated as literal integral tangents. Choose the 69 coordinate directions of the invertible minor and the two essential kernel directions. Their span is a 71-dimensional affine slice transverse to the 19 presentation directions. Solving 69 equations by the algebraic implicit function theorem leaves one equation in two variables with nondegenerate quadratic term \(q\). The slice is therefore an ordinary nodal curve, with two actual algebraic branches. The common-root test says that both branches smooth all three nodes of \(C_0\). Properness and openness of smoothness exclude new singularities elsewhere. Each general fiber is consequently a smooth connected genus-four curve on the same \(T\).

Choose the slope \(\alpha=19+8v\) modulo 23. It satisfies \(q(1,\alpha)=0\) and \(\partial_tq(1,\alpha)=v\ne0\). Over characteristic zero, choose the simple root of the lifted quadratic with this reduction. The 69-minor and this derivative are units at the chosen place. Recursive solution of the fixed equation \(\Phi(z(t))=G\) therefore uses only unit denominators and reduces to the verifier's series. The equation \(G\) is held fixed throughout this recurrence.

Along the punctured branch \(d\Phi\) has rank 70. There is actual curve motion because the slice is transverse to presentation changes. Consequently the normal cokernel is nonzero, its positive part is zero, and its negative ideal has rank at most 59. The verifier finds a first-order increase from 58 to 59, so this rank is exactly 59 over the branch function field.

To obtain \(\ell(t)\), solve the 58 independent ideal equations with their unit constant minor. An additional column gives a relation between the two resulting left-kernel vectors; it vanishes to order exactly one. Division by \(t\) is legitimate because the central rank is exactly 58 in characteristic zero. The rank-59 bound then makes the resulting functional annihilate every ideal column at every order. It also annihilates the fixed Jacobian ideal, since differentiating \(G=f_1g_1+f_2g_2+hk\) puts every derivative of \(G\) in \(I\).

The verifier checks the required fixed-equation coefficients through order 49, all 72 ideal columns and all 12 negative Jacobian directions through order 47, and the nonzero 48-minor. Unit denominators make the same minor nonzero in characteristic zero. This proves the full span in (3B.4.1), rather than merely a nonzero Abel–Jacobi image.

It also checks the normalization in (3B.3.4). After eliminating \(u\), the four forms \((f_2,h,g_1,g_2)\) have degrees \((2,3,4,4)\), with quotient dimensions one in degree nine and zero in degree ten. They are a regular sequence. At the initial branch tangent,

\[
\eta_R/dt=17v\,\ell_0(R)\pmod{23}.
\]

This nonzero scalar makes the common normalization a formal unit. Thus the first 48 normalized coefficient rows have the same rank; no additional high-order residue calculation is needed.

## 3B.5 Openness in the full weighted family

The preceding calculation proves surjectivity on one fixed threefold. To obtain an open family of such threefolds, use actual smooth points of its contact parameter curve. Their obstruction lines span the 48-dimensional dual: otherwise a constant nonzero class would annihilate all of them and hence every formal coefficient. Choose 48 points with independent lines, where \(d\Phi\) has rank 70 and \(h^0N=h^1N=1\).

Let \(\mathcal S\) be the smooth open of the full 70-dimensional space \(S_6^+\), and let \(\mathcal P\) be the open of norm presentations satisfying these rank and smoothness conditions. The map \(\mathcal P\to\mathcal S\) is smooth. The obstruction line is algebraic in the dual of the rank-48 Jacobian bundle. In the 48-fold fiber product of \(\mathcal P\) over \(\mathcal S\), independence of these lines is a Zariski-open condition. This open contains the selected tuple. Smooth morphisms are open, so its image contains a nonempty Zariski open \(\mathcal U\subset\mathcal S\).

For every member of \(\mathcal U\), each selected presentation lies on an actual local Hilbert curve: the fixed-equation fiber has dimension 20, its presentation fibers have dimension 19, and \(h^0N=1\). Complete and normalize these parameter curves. Their combined pullback on \(H^{2,1}(T)^-\) is injective by the 48 independent tangent lines. They may belong to different components; take their finite disjoint union. Conjugation and duality give a surjective curve correspondence onto \(H^3(T)^-\) for every member of \(\mathcal U\).

## 3B.6 Supported projectors and specialization

To apply the supported-projector specialization lemma of [Chapter 3, §3.6](#technical-information/geometric-support), we first produce the required cycle on the square of a divisor. The anti-projector acts on the single primitive degree \(H^3(T)^-\), and the preceding curve correspondences surject onto that degree on a nonempty Zariski open of the parameter space. Its transpose supplies the polarization adjoint.

In this case, replace \(\Gamma\) by \(P^-\circ\Gamma\), choose a \(\sigma\)-stable divisor \(D\) containing its image, and set \(S=\Gamma\circ{}^t\Gamma\). The polarization on \(H^1(\Lambda)(-1)\) and the primitive polarization on \(H^3(T)\) make \({}^t\Gamma\) the adjoint up to a fixed nonzero sign. Surjectivity makes \(S|_{H^3(T)^-}\) invertible. On all other cohomology it is zero. If its rational characteristic polynomial is \(t^m+a_{m-1}t^{m-1}+\cdots+a_0\), then \(a_0\ne0\) and

\[
[P^-]=-\frac{[S^m]+a_{m-1}[S^{m-1}]+\cdots+a_1[S]}{a_0}
\quad\text{in }H^6(T\times T,\mathbb Q).
\]

Every term has a cycle representative supported on \(D\times D\). Equality of all cohomological actions implies equality of classes by Künneth and Poincaré duality. Thus the inverse is a polynomial in an existing algebraic correspondence; no algebraic inverse conjecture is needed.

The family of smooth invariant weighted sextics is connected. The shared specialization lemma now applies: the projector is algebraic throughout the family, and it has a supported representative on a nonempty Zariski open, hence at very general fibers. Proper relative flag Hilbert schemes give such a representative at every smooth member. Fixed Hilbert polynomials keep the limiting support a divisor, and the flag conditions keep the limiting cycle on its square. Acting on cohomology proves the weighted threefold theorem.

This step includes the cyclic covers \(u^3=h(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)\). They lie in a special subfamily, so this inclusion uses the all-smooth specialization step rather than an openness assertion within the cyclic subfamily.

## 3B.7 The two-reflection support theorem

**Two-reflection support theorem.** Let \(X=(F=0)\subset\mathbb P^5\) be smooth, with coordinates \((X_0,X_1,s,Y_0,Y_1,t)\). Suppose \(F\) is invariant under

\[
\tau:(X,Y)\mapsto(X,-Y),\qquad
r_s:s\mapsto-s,\qquad r_t:t\mapsto-t.
\]

Then \(H^4(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau\subset N^1H^4(X,\mathbb Q)\).

**Proof.** The reflection theorem of [§3.3](#technical-information/geometric-support/33-reflection-quotients) supports \(H^4(X)^{r_s=+}\) and \(H^4(X)^{r_t=+}\): each quotient is a smooth Fano sextic in \(\mathbb P(1^5,2)\). Its weighted vertex is absent because the relevant pure sixth-power coefficient is nonzero; otherwise the corresponding coordinate-axis point would be singular on \(X\). The branch divisor is smooth and the quotient action is a reflection in its normal direction.

It remains to support the simultaneous character

\[
V_{--}=H^4(X)^{\tau=+,\ r_s=-,\ r_t=-}.
\]

Put \(\beta=r_sr_t\) and \(\sigma=\tau r_t\). On this subspace \(\beta=+\) and \(\sigma=-\). The latter involution negates precisely \(Y_0,Y_1\), fixing \(X_0,X_1,s,t\).

Write \(x=(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)\). The pencil \([s:t]\) has base

\[
S=X\cap(s=t=0)=\{h_6(x)=0\}\subset\mathbb P^3.
\]

Both binary derivatives vanish there by separate evenness. A singular point of \(S\) would therefore be singular on \(X\), so \(S\) is smooth. Blow up \(S\) to obtain a morphism to \(\mathbb P^1\). Bertini gives smooth general fibers

\[
V_\lambda=\{F(x,s,\lambda s)=0\}\subset\mathbb P^4.
\]

All pencil members are smooth along their base surface, where the core gradient is nonzero. Blowing up restricts to an isomorphism on a smooth fiber because \(S\) is a Cartier divisor in it.

The involution \(\beta\) fixes \(\lambda\) and acts on \(V_\lambda\) by \(s\mapsto-s\). With \(w=s^2\), its quotient is

\[
T_\lambda:
h_6(x)+w h_4(x,\lambda)+w^2h_2(x,\lambda)+w^3h_0(\lambda)=0
\subset\mathbb P(1,1,1,1,2).
\]

Each core coefficient is invariant under \(\sigma\). The binary restriction \(F(0,s,t)\) is nonzero and squarefree: separate evenness forces every core monomial degree to be even, so all core first derivatives vanish on the binary line; a zero restriction or a multiple root would make \(X\) singular. Excluding its roots makes \(h_0(\lambda)\ne0\), so the weighted vertex is absent. The only remaining fixed locus of \(\beta\) in a fiber is the smooth branch surface \(s=0\), where it is a reflection. Thus, after removing finitely many parameters and one affine-chart boundary, the quotients form a smooth projective family \(p:\mathcal T\to U\) of the weighted threefolds just treated.

The relative support lemma of [Chapter 3, §3.6](#technical-information/geometric-support) now applies. Its two requirements are

\[
(R^jp_*\mathbb Q)^-=0\quad(j\ne3),
\qquad
P^-_\lambda\text{ has a representative supported on }D_\lambda\times D_\lambda.
\]

The second is the weighted threefold theorem, including special members. For the first, finite quotient cohomology identifies \(H^j(T_\lambda)\) with the \(\beta\)-invariants in \(H^j(V_\lambda)\). Ordinary weak Lefschetz and duality on the smooth sextic \(V_\lambda\) make all its nonmiddle cohomology invariant under \(\sigma\).

The shared lemma therefore supports

\[
H^4(\mathcal T)^-=H^1(U,(R^3p_*\mathbb Q)^-)
\]

on a horizontal divisor. Its spread and finite-trace argument supplies the relative cycle; no choice of a continuously varying divisor is assumed here.

For \(\alpha\in V_{--}\), pull back to the blowup and restrict over \(U\). Its \(\beta\)-invariance identifies it with the pullback of a class on the finite quotient \(\mathcal T\), and its \(\sigma\)-character is negative. Hence it vanishes off the inverse image of the supporting divisor. Taking closures and adding the omitted fibers and exceptional divisor supports the pullback on the blowup. Proper birational pushforward supports \(\alpha\) on \(X\). Together with the two Fano-supported sectors, this exhausts \(H^4(X)^\tau\). ∎

## 3B.8 Scope, examples and certificates

The theorem covers the entire smooth locus of a 104-coefficient linear family, of projective dimension 103 before changes of coordinates. The spaces of core forms of degrees \(6,4,2,0\), even in \((Y_0,Y_1)\), have dimensions \(44,19,6,1\). The powers \(s^{2a}t^{2b}\) with \(a+b=m\) give \(m+1\) choices, so the coefficient count is

\[
44+2\cdot19+3\cdot6+4\cdot1=104.
\]

The coordinate orbit and comparison with other supported families are discussed in [Chapter 4](#technical-information/known-locus). The Fano quotient results remain part of the theorem: they supply the sectors with either reflection positive, while the weighted family supplies the simultaneous negative sector.

The two-reflection and [quadratic-net families](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) are incomparable, even after block-linear changes. In the bidegree-\((4,2)\) part of a general two-reflection equation, the quadrics appearing as coefficients of \(X\)-quartics span the four-dimensional space
\[
\langle Y_0^2,Y_0Y_1,Y_1^2,t^2\rangle.
\]
A presentation through three \(Y\)-quadrics would bound this rank by three; the mirrored bidegree-\((2,4)\) calculation excludes an \(X\)-quadric presentation. Conversely, the 127-dimensional saturated net family cannot be contained in the 111-dimensional saturated two-reflection family. These dimensions are proved in Chapter 4.

Two immediate applications illustrate the coefficient scope.

- If \(F=h(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)+b(s,t)\), with \(h\) even in \((Y_0,Y_1)\) and \(b\) even in \(t\), homogeneity makes \(b\) even in \(s\). Thus every smooth member of this \(4+2\) split family is covered, including a sum of two arbitrary same-parity binary sextics and a separately even binary sextic. That binary-block subfamily also admits the torsion-contact construction of [Chapter 2A](#technical-information/binary-blocks), which gives explicit fields through two general Wronskian spanning theorems.
- If an even sextic is invariant under an \(X\)-coordinate transposition and an independent \(Y\)-coordinate transposition, their sums and differences diagonalize them over \(\mathbb Q\) to the required reflections. Block-symmetric even sextics therefore satisfy the theorem after such a coordinate change.

Over a characteristic-zero field, the support-to-certificate equivalence and coefficient descent of [Chapter 1](#technical-information/certificates), followed by the higher-pole reduction of [Chapter 3, §3.5](#technical-information/geometric-support), give legal certificates at every positive pole order.

The two extra reflections are essential hypotheses of this proof. Global \(Y\)-evenness alone does not provide either the weighted quotient fibers or their two-minus core involution.

# 3B. Weighted threefolds and two-reflection sextics

[Previous: split sextics and K3 correspondences](#technical-information/split-and-k3) · [Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: quadratic nets and pair correspondences](#technical-information/quadratic-nets)

A smooth even sextic with one additional reflection in an \(X\)-coordinate and one in a \(Y\)-coordinate has its entire invariant fourth cohomology supported on a divisor. The individual reflection quotients are Fano and supply the sectors where either reflection acts positively. The remaining simultaneous negative sector comes from a family of weighted Calabi–Yau threefolds. This chapter proves the required threefold theorem and the passage from its fibers to the fourfold.

The proof constructs genus-four curves whose sums with their involution translates are complete intersections of two quadrics. Their normal sequence computes the Abel–Jacobi differential, and a finite exact spanning calculation supplies a surjective curve correspondence. Openness and a supported projector then extend the result to every smooth member. This retains the curve-correspondence strategy of [Voisin, Proposition 2.1](https://www.numdam.org/item/ASNSP_1992_4_19_4_473_0.pdf), with an explicit contact construction supplying the curves. We work over \(\mathbb C\) with rational cohomology; coefficient descent is addressed at the end.

## 3B.1 The weighted threefold theorem

Let

\[
T\subset\mathbb P(1,1,1,1,2),\qquad
\sigma(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1,u)=(x_0,x_1,-y_0,-y_1,u).
\]

**Weighted threefold theorem.** Suppose \(T\) is a quasismooth degree-six hypersurface with \(\sigma\)-invariant equation. Then

\[
H^3(T,\mathbb Q)^-\subset N^1H^3(T,\mathbb Q).
\]

More precisely, the algebraic anti-projector

\[
P^-=(\Delta_T-\Gamma_\sigma)/2
\]

is cohomologous to a rational algebraic cycle supported on \(D\times D\) for some divisor \(D\subset T\).

Quasismoothness forces the coefficient of \(u^3\) to be nonzero. Otherwise every partial derivative of the cone equation vanishes at a nonzero point of the \(u\)-axis. Thus \(T\) avoids the unique weighted singular vertex and is an ordinary smooth projective threefold. Weighted adjunction gives \(K_T\simeq\mathcal O_T\). The determinant of \(\sigma\) is positive, so \(H^{3,0}(T)\) is invariant and the minus part has types \((2,1)+(1,2)\). This Hodge-theoretic coniveau does not itself give the divisor; the proof below constructs the required algebraic image.

Weighted weak Lefschetz and duality give

\[
H^1(T)=H^5(T)=0,\qquad
H^2(T)=\mathbb Qh,\qquad H^4(T)=\mathbb Qh^2.
\]

Consequently \(P^-\) acts only on \(H^3(T)^-\). The weighted residue and Lefschetz statements used here and below are in [Dolgachev, §§3.2–3.3 and 4.2–4.3](https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/idolga/wp-content/uploads/sites/1334/2024/08/weighted82.pdf).

## 3B.2 Genus-four norm contacts

Write \(S=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,u]\), with weights \((1,1,1,1,2)\), and let \(\sigma\) negate \(c,d\). Superscripts indicate its eigenspaces. Consider the polynomial map

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi:(S_2^+)^2\times(S_4^+)^2\times S_3^+\times S_3^-
&\longrightarrow S_6^+,\\
(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2,A,B)&\longmapsto
f_1g_1+f_2g_2+A^2-B^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Its source has dimension \(2\cdot7+2\cdot26+12+12=90\), and its target has dimension 70. Put \(h=A+B\), \(k=A-B=\sigma h\). A presentation \(G=\Phi(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2,A,B)\) gives curves

\[
C=(f_1=f_2=h=0),\qquad
\sigma C=(f_1=f_2=k=0)
\]

on \(T=(G=0)\). We call this a **norm contact**, since \(hk=h\sigma h\). On the open where these are complete intersections,

\[
C+\sigma C=T\cap(f_1=f_2=0)\sim4h_{\mathrm{hyp}}^2.
\qquad\text{(3B.2.1)}
\]

Assume one quadric has a nonzero \(u\)-coefficient. Eliminating \(u\) identifies \(C\) with an ordinary complete intersection of degrees \((2,3)\) in \(\mathbb P^3\). If \(C\) is smooth, adjunction gives

\[
K_C=\mathcal O_C(1),\qquad \deg\mathcal O_C(1)=6,\qquad g(C)=4.
\]

**Construction from a cubic-surface line.** Suppose
\[
G=A^2-B^2+H(q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3),
\qquad q_i\in S_2^+,\quad A\in S_3^+,\quad B\in S_3^-,
\]
where \(H\) is an ordinary cubic form. A line \(L=(\ell_1=\ell_2=0)\) on \(H=0\) gives \(H=\ell_1H_1+\ell_2H_2\), with quadratic \(H_i\). Pulling back supplies the norm presentation
\[
f_i=\ell_i(q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3),\qquad
g_i=H_i(q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3).
\]
This replaces a search for all six contact forms by a line calculation on a cubic surface. The pulled-back curve must still be a smooth complete intersection with the stated \(u\)-coefficient condition; the line alone does not imply these properties or the normal-rank and spanning conditions below.

### Presentation changes and actual curve motion

For a fixed embedded curve \(C\) and a fixed equation \(G\), the presentation fiber has dimension 19 on this open. There are four parameters for changing the basis \(f_1,f_2\), eight for replacing

\[
h\longmapsto h+f_1\ell_1+f_2\ell_2,
\qquad \ell_i\in S_1,
\]

and seven for the syzygy

\[
(g_1,g_2)\longmapsto(g_1+f_2q,g_2-f_1q),\qquad q\in S_2^+.
\]

There is no further continuous scaling of \(h\): modulo \((f_1,f_2)\), the identity \(G=h\sigma h\ne0\) forces that scaling to have square one. Conversely, the minimal complete-intersection generators show that these are all presentation changes. Thus, where \(d\Phi\) is surjective, its 20-dimensional fixed-\(G\) fiber supplies a genuine one-dimensional family of curves.

### An intrinsic chart

The same incidence has a smaller description useful for explicit finite-cover constructions. On the chart where the quadrics' \(u\) and \(ab\) coefficients are independent, choose their basis so that

\[
f_1=u+Q_1,\qquad
f_2=Q_2=ab+\lambda a^2+\mu b^2+q(c,d),
\]

where \(Q_1\) has no \(ab\) term. Each quadric has five free coefficients. Reduce the cubics \(A,B\) modulo \(Q_2\), using monomials not divisible by \(ab\). There are eight such monomials of each parity, giving \(5+5+8+8=26\) parameters.

This reduction is defined on a precise open chart. Put \(z=\lambda\mu\). The determinant for cubic reduction is \(1-z\); the determinant for invariant sextic reduction is

\[
\Delta=(1-z)(1-3z)(1-2z)^3.
\qquad\text{(3B.2.2)}
\]

To check this, project multiplication by \(Q_2\) onto monomials divisible by \(ab\). Ordering by the \(c,d\)-degree gives triangular blocks with tridiagonal determinants \(D_m=D_{m-1}-zD_{m-2}\), \(D_0=D_1=1\). In degree six the blocks are \(D_5=(1-z)(1-3z)\), three copies of \(D_3=1-2z\), and five copies of \(D_1\). The degree-three blocks give \(1-z\).

On \(\Delta\ne0\), the condition for a fixed invariant weighted sextic is

\[
\operatorname{rem}_{Q_2}\!\left(G(a,b,c,d,-Q_1)-A^2+B^2\right)=0.
\qquad\text{(3B.2.3)}
\]

The invariant sextic quotient has dimension \(44-19=25\), so this is a system of 25 equations in 26 parameters. For a cyclic equation \(G=u^3+H\), its argument is \(H-Q_1^3-A^2+B^2\).

Suppose a curve component of this incidence has universal surface dominating the ratio plane \(r=b/a, s=d/c\). On \(a=1, c=t, d=st\), a moving point is specified by (3B.2.3) and

\[
Q_2(1,r,t,st)=0,\qquad
(A+B)(1,r,t,st)=0,\qquad u=-Q_1(1,r,t,st).
\]

There are 27 equations in the 26 parameters and \(t\), over \(\mathbb C(r,s)\). Dominance, rather than this equation count alone, makes the resulting component generically finite; in characteristic zero it is generically étale. This supplies a finite algebraic moving-point field for the differential and trace constructions of [Chapter 2, §2.8](#technical-information/explicit-constructions). The closed forms needed there come from the next section.

## 3B.3 Normal obstructions and residue forms

### The normal sequence and the correspondence pairing

For a smooth norm-contact curve, the normal sequence is

\[
0\longrightarrow N_{C/T}\longrightarrow
E:=\mathcal O_C(2)^2\oplus\mathcal O_C(3)
\xrightarrow{(g_1,g_2,k)}\mathcal O_C(6)
\longrightarrow0.
\qquad\text{(3B.3.1)}
\]

Riemann–Roch gives \(h^0(E)=h^0(\mathcal O_C(6))=33\) and \(H^1(E)=0\). Complete-intersection restriction maps are surjective. Hence

\[
H^1(N_{C/T})\simeq
S_6/(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2,A,B)_6,
\qquad h^0(N_{C/T})=h^1(N_{C/T}).
\qquad\text{(3B.3.2)}
\]

The invariant part of the displayed ideal is exactly the image of \(d\Phi\). If \(d\Phi\) has rank 70 and the negative part of this ideal has codimension one, then \(h^0N=h^1N=1\). The actual family from §3B.2 is therefore a smooth local Hilbert curve.

Choose the residue volume form \(\Omega_T=\operatorname{Res}_T(\Omega_{\mathbb P}/G)\). It identifies \(T_T\simeq\Omega_T^2\) and \(\det N_{C/T}\simeq K_C\). For a deformation \(\kappa\in H^1(T,T_T)\), let \(\rho_C(\kappa)\in H^1(C,N_{C/T})\) be the obstruction to carrying \(C\) along that deformation. Let \(\Lambda\) be the smooth projective completion of a parameter curve and \(\Gamma\subset\Lambda\times T\) its closed universal correspondence. For a tangent vector \(D\) at a smooth member, with normal velocity \(v_D\), the correspondence pullback satisfies

\[
\bigl(\Gamma^*(\kappa\mathbin{\lrcorner}\Omega_T)\bigr)(D)
=\operatorname{Tr}_C\bigl(v_D\wedge\rho_C(\kappa)\bigr),
\qquad\text{(3B.3.3)}
\]

with compatible wedge conventions. Indeed, pullback by the universal curve followed by integration over its fibers evaluates the left side by contracting the \((2,1)\)-form with the normal velocity. Restricting a Dolbeault representative of \(\kappa\) to \(C\) gives its normal obstruction; contraction with \(\Omega_T\) turns the resulting integrand into the Serre pairing on the right. This is the infinitesimal Abel–Jacobi pairing, expressed entirely on the smooth threefold and its curve; see [Westhoff, pp. 375–377 and §3](https://msp.org/pjm/1998/183-2/pjm-v183-n2-p08-s.pdf) for the contraction description and its reduction to residues.

The Euler and normal sequences identify \(H^1(T,T_T)\) with the degree-six Jacobian ring

\[
R_6(G)=\bigl(S/(G_a,G_b,G_c,G_d,G_u)\bigr)_6.
\]

Under (3B.3.2), \(\rho_C\) is the quotient map on polynomial deformations. The map is surjective, so its Serre transpose is injective on \(H^0(N_{C/T})\). In particular, nonzero curve motion has nonzero Abel–Jacobi derivative. Relation (3B.2.1) places this derivative in the negative sector.

### A canonical residue formula

There is an algebraic normalization of (3B.3.3). Suppose \(g_1,g_2\) have no common zero on \(C\), equivalently the sequence

\[
\mathbf f=(f_1,f_2,h,g_1,g_2)
\]

is regular in \(S\). Its weighted degrees are \((2,2,3,4,4)\), so its Artinian quotient has length 96 and socle degree 9. Let \(\tau_{\mathbf f}\) be its Grothendieck residue, normalized by

\[
\tau_{\mathbf f}\!\left(
\det\frac{\partial(f_1,f_2,h,g_1,g_2)}
{\partial(a,b,c,d,u)}\right)=96.
\]

For a fixed negative sextic \(R\) and a family of contacts on the fixed threefold \(T\), the corresponding one-form on the parameter curve is, up to one overall sign convention,

\[
\boxed{\qquad \eta_R=\tau_{\mathbf f}(R\,d_\Lambda h).\qquad}
\qquad\text{(3B.3.4)}
\]

Here \(d_\Lambda\) differentiates coefficients while holding the ambient coordinates fixed. The degree is \(6+3=9\), as required.

For completeness, on the cover \(g_1\ne0, g_2\ne0\), lifts of \(R|_C\) through (3B.3.1) are \((R/g_1,0,0)\) and \((0,R/g_2,0)\). Their difference represents the obstruction. If \(v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)\), then \(g_1v_1+g_2v_2+kv_3=0\), and its Serre pairing is represented by

\[
\frac{Rv_3}{g_1g_2}\,\theta_C,
\qquad
\theta_C=\operatorname{Res}_C\frac{\Omega_{\mathbb P}}{f_1f_2h}.
\]

The adjunction form \(\theta_C\) has twist \(K_C\otimes\mathcal O_C(-1)\), canceled by the degree-one coefficient. Its Serre trace is exactly the residue above; the actual velocity has \(v_3=-D(h)\). This proves (3B.3.4), including a constant normalization rather than an unspecified function of the parameter.

If \(f_1=\lambda u+q\), eliminating \(u\) contributes \(1/\lambda\) to the four-variable residue. One differentiates \(h\) first and then substitutes \(u=-q/\lambda\); differentiating the already substituted cubic gives a different expression. At nonreduced intersections the Artinian residue remains valid without division by a pointwise Jacobian.

On \(\Lambda\), these forms extend holomorphically because they equal \(\Gamma^*H^{2,1}(T)^-\). They are therefore closed. Once the pullback is injective, the polarization argument in §3B.6 makes \(\Gamma_*\Gamma^*\) invertible on the negative sector. Thus these canonical forms suffice to recover every source after applying that inverse. The identity \(\Gamma_*\eta_R=R\) does not follow without this inversion; the moving-point trace formula still requires its exact differential correction.

## 3B.4 A finite spanning criterion and an exact witness

### The criterion

Weighted residues give

\[
H^{2,1}(T)^-\simeq R_6(G)^-,\qquad \dim R_6(G)^-=48.
\]

For example, at the weighted Fermat equation the ring is
\(\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,u]/(a^5,b^5,c^5,d^5,u^2)\); its negative degree-six monomials have dimensions 32 without \(u\) and 16 with \(u\). The dimensions are constant throughout the smooth invariant family.

Suppose a nonconstant algebraic family of curves on a fixed \(T\) has smooth general member, \(h^0N=h^1N=1\), and a nonzero formal obstruction functional

\[
\ell(t)\in\bigl(R_6(G)^-\bigr)^\vee((t)).
\]

By (3B.3.3), this functional differs from the actual correspondence differential by a common nonzero meromorphic scalar. If its coefficient rows span the 48-dimensional dual, then

\[
\Gamma^*:H^{2,1}(T)^-\hookrightarrow H^{1,0}(\Lambda).
\qquad\text{(3B.4.1)}
\]

Indeed, a constant class in the kernel is killed by every coefficient row. Conjugation and Poincaré duality then give

\[
\Gamma_*:H^1(\Lambda)(-1)\twoheadrightarrow H^3(T)^-.
\qquad\text{(3B.4.2)}
\]

In particular \(g(\Lambda)\ge48\). It is the genus of the parameter curve, not the genus four of its fibers, that appears in this inequality. A nodal member is allowed at \(t=0\); the pairing is applied on the smooth punctured branch.

### A smooth algebraic norm presentation

We construct one smooth threefold and one contact family satisfying the criterion. Put

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta(x,y,u)&=2x^6+y^6+30x^4u+30x^2u^2+2u^3,\\
Q_x&=a^2+2ab-u,\qquad Q_y=c^2+2cd-u,\\
G&=\Theta(a,b,u)+\Theta(c,d,u)
       +\frac57Q_x^2Q_y+\frac{10}{7}Q_xQ_y^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Modulo five, this is \(2a^6+b^6+2c^6+d^6+4u^3\). Its affine cone is smooth away from the origin, proving quasismoothness in characteristic zero by properness of the singular locus. The nonzero \(u^3\)-coefficient excludes the weighted vertex, so \(T=(G=0)\) is smooth.

The square completion

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_x&=(2a+b)^2,\qquad
R_x=(a^2-u)b+(2a+b)^3-2(2a+b)Q_x,\\
S_y&=(2c+d)^2,\qquad
R_y=(c^2-u)d+(2c+d)^3-2(2c+d)Q_y,\\
\Psi(S,Q)&=-2S^3+6S^2Q-3SQ^2-2Q^3
\end{aligned}
\]

gives \(\Theta(a,b,u)=3R_x^2+\Psi(S_x,Q_x)\), and similarly for \(c,d\). Thus

\[
G=3R_x^2+3R_y^2+H(S_x,Q_x,S_y,Q_y),
\quad
H(S,Q,T,V)=\Psi(S,Q)+\Psi(T,V)+\frac57Q^2V+\frac{10}{7}QV^2.
\]

Choose a graph line on this cubic surface by imposing the four coefficient equations

\[
H(S,Q,kS+lQ,nS+mQ)\equiv0.
\]

They have the simple solution

\[
(k,l,n,m)\equiv(2,-3,-2,15)\pmod{37},
\]

where their Jacobian determinant is \(3\). Hensel's lemma gives a unique lift in these residue classes. The invertible Jacobian makes this an isolated algebraic solution, so its coordinates lie in a number field with a place over 37. Adjoin the simple roots \(i^2=-1\), \((\sqrt3)^2=3\), choosing \(i\equiv6\), \(\sqrt3\equiv15\) at that place.

Set \(T_0=kS_x+lQ_x\), \(V_0=nS_x+mQ_x\), and use the cubic-surface construction of §3B.2:

\[
\begin{aligned}
f_1&=S_y-T_0,&f_2&=Q_y-V_0,\\
A&=\sqrt3R_x,&B&=i\sqrt3R_y,\\
g_1&=\frac{H(S_x,Q_x,S_y,Q_y)-H(S_x,Q_x,T_0,Q_y)}{S_y-T_0},\\
g_2&=\frac{H(S_x,Q_x,T_0,Q_y)-H(S_x,Q_x,T_0,V_0)}{Q_y-V_0}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The two divided differences are polynomials, of weighted degree four. These forms satisfy \(G=f_1g_1+f_2g_2+A^2-B^2\) over the number field, with the required characters. The equation \(G\) itself remains the displayed rational polynomial.

The exact verifier `scripts/verify-norm-contact-span.py`, in the repository's [reproduction scripts](https://github.com/hodge-computer/sextics/tree/main/scripts), reconstructs this presentation, its coefficient matrices, tangent direction and formal coefficients from the defining equations. It reads no witness data. It uses lexicographically ordered weighted monomials and exact arithmetic in \(\mathbb F_{37}\). Run it with Python and NumPy:

```sh
python3 scripts/verify-norm-contact-span.py
```

The finite results needed in the proof are:

| Calculation modulo 37 | Result |
| --- | --- |
| \(d\Phi\) at the presentation | rank 70; a 70-minor is 21 |
| Negative degree-six ideal \(I_6^-\), \(I=(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2,A,B)\) | rank 59; a 59-minor is 4 |
| Singular ideal of the eliminated \((2,3)\) curve, degree six | rank 84 of 84 |
| \((f_1,f_2,A+B,g_1,g_2)\), weighted degree ten | rank 581 of 581 |
| 70 pivot directions, one essential tangent and 19 presentation directions | determinant 10 |
| First 48 obstruction coefficient rows | rank 48; a 48-minor is 17 |

The \(u\)-coefficient of \(f_1\) is \(l\), a unit at the chosen place. Eliminating \(u\) identifies \(C_0=(f_1=f_2=A+B=0)\) with an ordinary \((2,3)\) complete intersection. Its singular ideal consists of those two equations and the six two-by-two Jacobian minors. Containing every degree-six monomial excludes a projective singular point over the algebraic closure. The unit minor proves the same in characteristic zero. Thus \(C_0\) is a smooth connected genus-four curve. The degree-ten calculation makes the five-form ideal supported only at the affine origin, so its generators are a regular sequence. The residue formula of §3B.3 therefore applies on a neighborhood of this contact.

### A smooth branch and its full span

Let \(z_0\) be the 90 coefficients of the lifted presentation. Choose the 70 pivot coordinate directions of the displayed minor, collected in a matrix \(E\), and the first nullspace basis vector \(v\) outside the 19 presentation directions. Construct \(v\) in characteristic zero by fixing the same free coordinates and solving with the unit 70-minor. This gives a genuine tangent with the computed reduction; no modular vector is treated as a literal characteristic-zero tangent. The determinant 10 proves transversality to presentation changes, and reduction in the curve coordinate ring also verifies that the normal velocity is nonzero.

The fixed-equation fiber in this 71-dimensional affine slice is an actual smooth algebraic parameter curve, with local parametrization

\[
z(t)=z_0+tv+Ex(t),\qquad x(0)=x'(0)=0,
\qquad \Phi(z(t))=G.
\]

The algebraic implicit function theorem applies because \(d\Phi(z_0)E\) is invertible. Since \(\Phi\) is quadratic, each coefficient of \(x(t)\) is obtained by applying this one inverse matrix to the quadratic convolution of earlier coefficients. All denominators are units at the chosen place; neither factorials nor the coefficient order are inverted. The recurrence therefore reduces to the computation modulo 37 even beyond order 37. Smoothness of the embedded curves and nonzero normal motion persist near \(t=0\).

We also need a characteristic-zero upper bound on the negative ideal rank. Actual motion gives \(h^0(N_{C/T})\ge1\), and (3B.3.2) gives \(h^1N=h^0N\). The invariant cokernel vanishes because \(d\Phi\) has rank 70. Thus the negative ideal has rank at most 59. Its unit 59-minor proves equality, both at the seed and over the branch function field. In particular \(h^0N=h^1N=1\).

Normalize the left kernel of the \(60\)-by-\(72\) matrix \(I_6^-(t)\) by its unit 59-minor, fixing the remaining coordinate to one. The rank bound makes the resulting \(\ell(t)\) annihilate every ideal column to every order. It also annihilates the fixed Jacobian ideal: differentiating the identity \(G=f_1g_1+f_2g_2+(A+B)(A-B)\) puts every partial derivative of \(G\) in \(I(t)\). The negative degree-six Jacobian part has dimension 12: eight directions multiply the weight-five derivatives by opposite-character linear forms, and four multiply \(G_u\) by negative quadrics.

The verifier checks the fixed equation and all 72 ideal columns through order 50, annihilation of all 12 fixed Jacobian directions, and the nonzero minor of \(\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_{47}\). Unit denominators lift the minor 17 to a nonzero characteristic-zero minor. These rows consequently span the entire dual of \(R_6(G)^-\), proving (3B.4.1).

Finally, use the residue normalization \(\tau_{\mathbf f}(\det\partial\mathbf f)=96\) from §3B.3, where \(\mathbf f=(f_1,f_2,A+B,g_1,g_2)\). The degree-nine Artinian quotient is one-dimensional, and the verifier checks for every negative degree-six monomial \(R\) that

\[
\tau_{\mathbf f}\bigl(R\,\dot h\bigr)=14\ell_0(R)\pmod{37}.
\]

Thus the canonical one-form and the normalized obstruction series differ by a formal unit. Multiplication by that common unit preserves the rank of their first 48 coefficient rows. The criterion gives the surjection (3B.4.2) for this smooth contact family.

## 3B.5 Openness in the full weighted family

The smooth contact family just constructed proves surjectivity on one fixed threefold. To obtain an open family of such threefolds, choose smooth points of its parameter curve. Their obstruction lines span the 48-dimensional dual: otherwise a constant nonzero class would annihilate all of them and hence every formal coefficient. Choose 48 points with independent lines, where \(d\Phi\) has rank 70 and \(h^0N=h^1N=1\).

Let \(\mathcal S\) be the smooth open of the full 70-dimensional space \(S_6^+\), and let \(\mathcal P\) be the open of norm presentations satisfying these rank and smoothness conditions. The map \(\mathcal P\to\mathcal S\) is smooth. The obstruction line is algebraic in the dual of the rank-48 Jacobian bundle. In the 48-fold fiber product of \(\mathcal P\) over \(\mathcal S\), independence of these lines is a Zariski-open condition. This open contains the selected tuple. Smooth morphisms are open, so its image contains a nonempty Zariski open \(\mathcal U\subset\mathcal S\).

For every member of \(\mathcal U\), each selected presentation lies on an actual local Hilbert curve: the fixed-equation fiber has dimension 20, its presentation fibers have dimension 19, and \(h^0N=1\). Complete and normalize these parameter curves. Their combined pullback on \(H^{2,1}(T)^-\) is injective by the 48 independent tangent lines. They may belong to different components; take their finite disjoint union. Conjugation and duality give a surjective curve correspondence onto \(H^3(T)^-\) for every member of \(\mathcal U\).

## 3B.6 Supported projectors and specialization

To apply the supported-projector specialization lemma of [Chapter 3, §3.6](#technical-information/geometric-support), we first produce the required cycle on the square of a divisor. The anti-projector acts on the single primitive degree \(H^3(T)^-\), and the preceding curve correspondences surject onto that degree on a nonempty Zariski open of the parameter space. Its transpose supplies the polarization adjoint.

In this case, replace \(\Gamma\) by \(P^-\circ\Gamma\), choose a \(\sigma\)-stable divisor \(D\) containing its image, and set \(S=\Gamma\circ{}^t\Gamma\). The polarization on \(H^1(\Lambda)(-1)\) and the primitive polarization on \(H^3(T)\) make \({}^t\Gamma\) the adjoint up to a fixed nonzero sign. Surjectivity makes \(S|_{H^3(T)^-}\) invertible. On all other cohomology it is zero. If its rational characteristic polynomial is \(t^m+a_{m-1}t^{m-1}+\cdots+a_0\), then \(a_0\ne0\) and

\[
[P^-]=-\frac{[S^m]+a_{m-1}[S^{m-1}]+\cdots+a_1[S]}{a_0}
\quad\text{in }H^6(T\times T,\mathbb Q).
\]

Every term has a cycle representative supported on \(D\times D\). Equality of all cohomological actions implies equality of classes by Künneth and Poincaré duality. Thus the inverse is a polynomial in an existing algebraic correspondence; no algebraic inverse conjecture is needed.

The family of smooth invariant weighted sextics is connected. The shared specialization lemma now applies: the projector is algebraic throughout the family, and it has a supported representative on a nonempty Zariski open, hence at very general fibers. Proper relative flag Hilbert schemes give such a representative at every smooth member. Fixed Hilbert polynomials keep the limiting support a divisor, and the flag conditions keep the limiting cycle on its square. Acting on cohomology proves the weighted threefold theorem.

This step includes the cyclic covers \(u^3=h(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)\). They lie in a special subfamily, so this inclusion uses the all-smooth specialization step rather than an openness assertion within the cyclic subfamily.

## 3B.7 The two-reflection support theorem

**Two-reflection support theorem.** Let \(X=(F=0)\subset\mathbb P^5\) be smooth, with coordinates \((X_0,X_1,s,Y_0,Y_1,t)\). Suppose \(F\) is invariant under

\[
\tau:(X,Y)\mapsto(X,-Y),\qquad
r_s:s\mapsto-s,\qquad r_t:t\mapsto-t.
\]

Then \(H^4(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau\subset N^1H^4(X,\mathbb Q)\).

**Proof.** The reflection theorem of [§3.3](#technical-information/geometric-support/33-reflection-quotients) supports \(H^4(X)^{r_s=+}\) and \(H^4(X)^{r_t=+}\): each quotient is a smooth Fano sextic in \(\mathbb P(1^5,2)\). Its weighted vertex is absent because the relevant pure sixth-power coefficient is nonzero; otherwise the corresponding coordinate-axis point would be singular on \(X\). The branch divisor is smooth and the quotient action is a reflection in its normal direction.

It remains to support the simultaneous character

\[
V_{--}=H^4(X)^{\tau=+,\ r_s=-,\ r_t=-}.
\]

Put \(\beta=r_sr_t\) and \(\sigma=\tau r_t\). On this subspace \(\beta=+\) and \(\sigma=-\). The latter involution negates precisely \(Y_0,Y_1\), fixing \(X_0,X_1,s,t\).

Write \(x=(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)\). The pencil \([s:t]\) has base

\[
S=X\cap(s=t=0)=\{h_6(x)=0\}\subset\mathbb P^3.
\]

Both binary derivatives vanish there by separate evenness. A singular point of \(S\) would therefore be singular on \(X\), so \(S\) is smooth. Blow up \(S\) to obtain a morphism to \(\mathbb P^1\). Bertini gives smooth general fibers

\[
V_\lambda=\{F(x,s,\lambda s)=0\}\subset\mathbb P^4.
\]

All pencil members are smooth along their base surface, where the core gradient is nonzero. Blowing up restricts to an isomorphism on a smooth fiber because \(S\) is a Cartier divisor in it.

The involution \(\beta\) fixes \(\lambda\) and acts on \(V_\lambda\) by \(s\mapsto-s\). With \(w=s^2\), its quotient is

\[
T_\lambda:
h_6(x)+w h_4(x,\lambda)+w^2h_2(x,\lambda)+w^3h_0(\lambda)=0
\subset\mathbb P(1,1,1,1,2).
\]

Each core coefficient is invariant under \(\sigma\). The binary restriction \(F(0,s,t)\) is nonzero and squarefree: separate evenness forces every core monomial degree to be even, so all core first derivatives vanish on the binary line; a zero restriction or a multiple root would make \(X\) singular. Excluding its roots makes \(h_0(\lambda)\ne0\), so the weighted vertex is absent. The only remaining fixed locus of \(\beta\) in a fiber is the smooth branch surface \(s=0\), where it is a reflection. Thus, after removing finitely many parameters and one affine-chart boundary, the quotients form a smooth projective family \(p:\mathcal T\to U\) of the weighted threefolds just treated.

The relative support lemma of [Chapter 3, §3.6](#technical-information/geometric-support) now applies. Its two requirements are

\[
(R^jp_*\mathbb Q)^-=0\quad(j\ne3),
\qquad
P^-_\lambda\text{ has a representative supported on }D_\lambda\times D_\lambda.
\]

The second is the weighted threefold theorem, including special members. For the first, finite quotient cohomology identifies \(H^j(T_\lambda)\) with the \(\beta\)-invariants in \(H^j(V_\lambda)\). Ordinary weak Lefschetz and duality on the smooth sextic \(V_\lambda\) make all its nonmiddle cohomology invariant under \(\sigma\).

The shared lemma therefore supports

\[
H^4(\mathcal T)^-=H^1(U,(R^3p_*\mathbb Q)^-)
\]

on a horizontal divisor. Its spread and finite-trace argument supplies the relative cycle; no choice of a continuously varying divisor is assumed here.

For \(\alpha\in V_{--}\), pull back to the blowup and restrict over \(U\). Its \(\beta\)-invariance identifies it with the pullback of a class on the finite quotient \(\mathcal T\), and its \(\sigma\)-character is negative. Hence it vanishes off the inverse image of the supporting divisor. Taking closures and adding the omitted fibers and exceptional divisor supports the pullback on the blowup. Proper birational pushforward supports \(\alpha\) on \(X\). Together with the two Fano-supported sectors, this exhausts \(H^4(X)^\tau\). ∎

## 3B.8 Scope, examples and certificates

The theorem covers the entire smooth locus of a 104-coefficient linear family, of projective dimension 103 before changes of coordinates. The spaces of core forms of degrees \(6,4,2,0\), even in \((Y_0,Y_1)\), have dimensions \(44,19,6,1\). The powers \(s^{2a}t^{2b}\) with \(a+b=m\) give \(m+1\) choices, so the coefficient count is

\[
44+2\cdot19+3\cdot6+4\cdot1=104.
\]

The coordinate orbit and comparison with other supported families are discussed in [Chapter 4](#technical-information/known-locus). The Fano quotient results remain part of the theorem: they supply the sectors with either reflection positive, while the weighted family supplies the simultaneous negative sector.

The two-reflection and [quadratic-net families](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) are incomparable, even after block-linear changes. In the bidegree-\((4,2)\) part of a general two-reflection equation, the quadrics appearing as coefficients of \(X\)-quartics span the four-dimensional space
\[
\langle Y_0^2,Y_0Y_1,Y_1^2,t^2\rangle.
\]
A presentation through three \(Y\)-quadrics would bound this rank by three; the mirrored bidegree-\((2,4)\) calculation excludes an \(X\)-quadric presentation. Conversely, the 127-dimensional saturated net family cannot be contained in the 111-dimensional saturated two-reflection family. These dimensions are proved in Chapter 4.

Two immediate applications illustrate the coefficient scope.

- If \(F=h(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)+b(s,t)\), with \(h\) even in \((Y_0,Y_1)\) and \(b\) even in \(t\), homogeneity makes \(b\) even in \(s\). Thus every smooth member of this \(4+2\) split family is covered, including a sum of two arbitrary same-parity binary sextics and a separately even binary sextic. That binary-block subfamily also admits the torsion-contact construction of [Chapter 2A](#technical-information/binary-blocks), which gives explicit fields through two general Wronskian spanning theorems.
- If an even sextic is invariant under an \(X\)-coordinate transposition and an independent \(Y\)-coordinate transposition, their sums and differences diagonalize them over \(\mathbb Q\) to the required reflections. Block-symmetric even sextics therefore satisfy the theorem after such a coordinate change.

Over a characteristic-zero field, the support-to-certificate equivalence and coefficient descent of [Chapter 1](#technical-information/certificates), followed by the higher-pole reduction of [Chapter 3, §3.5](#technical-information/geometric-support), give legal certificates at every positive pole order.

The two extra reflections are essential hypotheses of this proof. Global \(Y\)-evenness alone does not provide either the weighted quotient fibers or their two-minus core involution.

# 4. Families, representations and deformation

[Previous: quadratic nets and pair correspondences](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) · [Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: computation](#technical-information/computation)

Support theorems have two kinds of hypotheses: restrictions on the coefficient family and restrictions on the cohomological representation. This chapter computes the dimensions of coefficient families, applies finite quotients and deck/exchange descent, and proves a criterion propagating one nonzero supported class over a dominant deformation family. The final section analyzes the representations of natural quotients and a dimension obstruction to an ordinary Fano-extension argument.

## 4.1 Coefficient spaces, Hodge structures and orbit dimensions

Write \(S=\mathbb C[X_{0},X_{1},X_{2},Y_{0},Y_{1},Y_{2}]\) and let \(\pm \) indicate total \(Y\)-parity. Counting by \(Y\)-degree gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{dim} S_{6}^{+} = 28+90+90+28 = 236,\\
\operatorname{dim} S_{6}^{-} = 63+100+63 = 226.
\end{gathered}
\]

Indeed, the summand of \(Y\)-degree \(j\) has dimension \(\binom{8-j}{2}\binom{j+2}{2}\). Hence the parameter space of even sextics is \(\mathbb P^{235}\). For smooth \(F\) its six quintic partial derivatives form a regular sequence: their affine common zero is only the origin, and a homogeneous system of parameters in a polynomial ring is regular. The Koszul resolution, with three even and three odd generators, gives the Hilbert and trace series

\[
\begin{gathered}
H(t) = (1+t+t^{2}+t^{3}+t^{4})^{6},\\
\Theta (t) = (1+t^{2}+t^{4}+t^{6}+t^{8})^{3},\\
\operatorname{dim} (R_F)_d^\pm  = ([t^{d}]H \pm  [t^{d}]\Theta )/2,\\
R_F = S/J(F).
\end{gathered}
\]

For example, the trace follows by dividing \((1-t^{5})^{3}(1+t^{5})^{3}\) by \((1-t)^{3}(1+t)^{3}\). Griffiths' residue identification from Chapter 1 therefore gives primitive invariant Hodge numbers \((208,866,208)\), in types \((3,1),(2,2),(1,3)\). In degree six, the same calculation is \(226-18=208\): the odd Jacobian directions are \(Y_{j}F_{X_{i}}\) and \(X_{i}F_{Y_{j}}\), and there are no linear syzygies among the quintic partials. The ambient \(h^{2}\) adds one algebraic middle direction.

Let \(G=GL_{3}(X)\times GL_{3}(Y)\), of dimension eighteen. For a linear coefficient family \(V\) preserved by a connected subgroup \(H\subset G\), the image of \(G\times V\to S_{6}\) has dimension at most \(\operatorname{dim} V+18-\operatorname{dim} H\): the action of \(H\) on the source, \((g,F)\mapsto(gh^{-1},hF)\), supplies fibres of dimension \(\operatorname{dim} H\). A matching differential rank at any point proves equality. At the Fermat member \(F_{0}=\sum Z_{i}^{6}\) the eighteen orbit derivatives are the distinct monomials \(6\cdot Z_{i}^{5}\cdot Z_{j}\), with \(i,j\) in the same parity block. Thus, for a monomial coefficient family containing \(F_{0}\), counting those derivatives outside \(V\) proves the required lower bound without a generic-rank assumption.

The same eighteen independent derivatives give affine orbit dimension eighteen at \(F_{0}\) and generically on each family below. Projectivization removes the common scalar direction, so the generic projective orbit has dimension seventeen. The equation-locus dimensions below include all block coordinate changes; their rational quotient dimensions are seventeen smaller. In particular, the ambient quotient has dimension 218.

Each family in the following table has \(H^4(X)^\tau\subset N^1H^4(X)\) throughout its smooth locus. The support mechanisms are proved in Chapters 3A–3C and §4.2 below.

| Smooth sextic family | Support mechanism | Projective equation locus | Quotient |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| \(G(X,Q_0(Y),Q_1(Y),Q_2(Y))\), or its \(X/Y\) mirror | Quadratic-net pair correspondence | 127 | 110 |
| One extra \(X\) reflection and one extra \(Y\) reflection | Fano quotients and weighted threefolds | 111 | 94 |
| Cyclic-six family of §4.2 | Deck/exchange descent | 91 | 74 |
| Block-sign split \(f(X)+g(Y)\) | Elliptic companions and contraction | 55 | 38 |
| Polarized split \(f(X+Y)+f(X-Y)\), with the order-three plane family | Algebraic Kuga–Satake correspondence | 24 | 7 |

The order-three family is \(f(z_0,z_1,z_2)=g_6(z_0,z_1)+z_2^3g_3(z_0,z_1)+a z_2^6\). The two-reflection theorem also applies to additive splittings and coordinate symmetries that give these reflections after a block-linear coordinate change, as described in [Chapter 3B](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds).

### Quadratic nets and recovery from the equation

Let \(N\subset S^2Y^*\) be a basepoint-free net. Its map of projective planes is finite and dominant, so the three quadratic generators are algebraically independent. For a fixed \(N\), the coefficient space is

\[
S^6X^*\oplus S^4X^*\otimes N
\oplus S^2X^*\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2N
\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^3N,
\]

of dimension \(28+15\cdot3+6\cdot6+10=119\). These spaces form a rank-119 vector subbundle of the trivial sextic bundle over the basepoint-free open subset of \(\operatorname{Gr}(3,6)\), of dimension nine. Its projectivization has dimension \(119+9-1=127\).

This is the dimension of the image, rather than only of its presentations. On the open set where the bidegree-\((4,2)\) contraction \(S^4X\to S^2Y^*\) has rank three, its image recovers \(N\). The recovery is regular on that rank locus. Basepoint-freeness is open, and membership of the remaining coefficient pieces in \(S^2X^*\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2N\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^3N\) is a closed condition in quotient bundles. Thus the smooth rank-three presentation locus is a quasiprojective subvariety of \(\mathbb P^{235}\), isomorphic to the corresponding open subset of the projective bundle. Its smooth locus is nonempty by the observation in Chapter 3C. The family is already \(G\)-stable, and its quotient dimension is \(127-17=110\).

**Example: diagonal nets.** Separate evenness in the three \(Y_i\) is composition through \(N=\langle Y_0^2,Y_1^2,Y_2^2\rangle\). Its coefficient space has projective dimension 118. The only rank-one conics in this net are the three coordinate squares, so its stabilizer in \(GL_3(Y)\) has dimension three. The net orbit has dimension six; hence this special locus has projective dimension \(119+6-1=124\), quotient dimension 107. Its full support is the diagonal-net corollary of Chapter 3C.

### The other coefficient families

For the two-reflection family, take the reflected coordinates to be \(X_2,Y_2\). Chapter 3B counts 104 coefficients. The preserving subgroup \(GL_2(X_0,X_1)\times G_m(X_2)\times GL_2(Y_0,Y_1)\times G_m(Y_2)\) has dimension ten. Exactly eight Fermat orbit derivatives mix a reflected coordinate with an unreflected coordinate in the same block, and lie outside the coefficient family. Thus its saturated cone has dimension \(104+8=112\), proving the projective dimensions \((103,111,94)\).

The cyclic-six family has 88 coefficients. Its preserving subgroup \(GL_3(X)\times GL_1(y)\times GL_2(z_0,z_1)\) has dimension fourteen. At Fermat, the four orbit monomials mixing \(y\) with \(z_0,z_1\) lie outside its invariant coefficient space. Its projective normal form therefore has dimension 87, its saturation dimension \(88+4-1=91\), and its quotient dimension 74.

The block-sign split family has \(28+28=56\) coefficients and is already \(G\)-stable, giving projective dimension 55 and quotient dimension 38.

For the polarized family, the twelve coefficients are \(7+4+1\). Put \(U=X+Y\) and \(V=X-Y\). At \(f=\sum z_{i}^{6}\) the family tangent consists of \(h(U)+h(V)\) for the twelve order-three monomials \(h\). A block-linear infinitesimal change in \(X,Y\) becomes

\[
\begin{gathered}
\delta U=C\cdot U+E\cdot V,     \delta V=C\cdot V+E\cdot U,\\
\delta F=6\sum _{i} [U_{i}^{5}(C\cdot U+E\cdot V)_{i}+V_{i}^{5}(C\cdot V+E\cdot U)_{i}],
\end{gathered}
\]

with arbitrary \(3\times 3\) matrices \(C,E\). The eighteen displayed directions are independent. The nine \(E\) directions have mixed \(U,V\) degree and do not meet the family tangent. Of the nine \(C\) directions, exactly five meet it: \(i,j\in \{0,1\}\), and \(i=j=2\). Thus the combined tangent dimension is \(12+18-5=25\). The simultaneous \(GL_{2}(z_{0},z_{1})\times G_{m}(z_{2})\), of dimension five, supplies the matching upper bound. Subtracting one for projectivization and seventeen for the generic orbit proves every entry in the table. All witnesses used here are smooth; for the polarized witness, the invertible \(U,V\) change reduces smoothness to Fermat. ∎

### Larger quadratic spaces

More generally, let \(N\subset S^2Y^*\) have dimension \(r\), and let \(b_r,c_r\) be the generic dimensions of its quadratic and cubic multiplication images. Sextics composed through \(N\) have coefficient-fiber dimension

\[
28+15r+6b_r+c_r.
\]

On the rank-\(r\) contraction locus the equation again recovers \(N\), so the projective image dimension is this number plus \(r(6-r)-1\). The resulting dimensions are

| \(r\) | \(b_r\) | \(c_r\) | Projective presentation locus |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 3 | 6 | 10 | 127 |
| 4 | 10 | 20 | 175 |
| 5 | 15 | 28 | 225 |
| 6 | 15 | 28 | 235 |

The multiplication ranks have elementary witnesses. For \(r=4\), take \(N=\langle x^2,y^2,z^2,xy+xz+yz\rangle\). Over \(\mathbb C(x^2,y^2,z^2)\), the fourth generator has four distinct conjugates under sign changes modulo simultaneous sign, and therefore minimal polynomial of degree four. There is no relation of degree at most three among the four generators, proving \(b_4=10,c_4=20\). For \(r=5\), take
\[
N=\langle xy,xz,yz,x^2-y^2,y^2-z^2\rangle.
\]
Its pairwise products span every quartic monomial: the cross-products give \(x^2y^2,x^2z^2,y^2z^2,xyz^2\) and their permutations; products of the two square differences give the pure fourth powers; multiplying a square difference by \(xy,xz,yz\) gives the remaining monomials. Thus \(N^2=S^4Y^*\). It follows that \(N^3=N S^4Y^*=S^6Y^*\): use \(S^4Y^*=N^2\subset N S^2Y^*\) and multiply by \(S^2Y^*\). Maximal rank is open, giving the generic values. The cases \(r=3,6\) are immediate from algebraic independence and the full quadratic space.

These are dimensions of presentation loci. The support theorem in Chapter 3C uses the degree-four map supplied by a net; larger multiplication images do not supply that theorem's geometric hypotheses. Its final section explains the change in the auxiliary threefolds.

## 4.2 Representations and surface quotients

A finite quotient transfers the image of its averaging projector. Divisor support for the quotient therefore need not support every cohomology class of the covering fourfold. For a polynomial map \(\Phi\), the weighted-Fano theorem of Chapter 3 identifies its residue image by the density condition \(A=\det(d\Phi)b(\Phi)\). The group-algebra formulation in §3.1 describes the corresponding restriction for finite symmetries.

For arbitrary smooth ternary \(f\), the polarized split decomposition of [Chapter 3A](#technical-information/split-and-k3) illustrates this distinction. It supports a rank-1073 substructure, including the ambient class, with primitive Hodge numbers \((189,694,189)\). The complementary rank-210 piece has Hodge numbers \((19,172,19)\) and is an exterior square of primitive K3 cohomology. Supporting this piece by the Kuga–Satake criterion requires algebraicity of that correspondence. The order-three family in §4.1 satisfies this additional hypothesis.

### A cyclic-six family and complementary quotients

The deck/exchange criterion of [Chapter 3, §3.1](#technical-information/geometric-support) can support an entire involution-invariant Hodge structure even when neither quotient alone supplies it. Let \(\zeta\) be a primitive sixth root and write the coordinates as \((X_0,X_1,X_2,y,z_0,z_1)\), with \(y,z_0,z_1\) the globally odd coordinates. Set

\[
g(X,y,z_0,z_1)=(X,\zeta y,\zeta^{-1}z_0,\zeta^{-1}z_1),
\qquad g^3=\tau.
\]

The complete \(g\)-invariant sextic family is

\[
F=f_6(X)+a y^6+P_6(z_0,z_1)
  +\sum_{m=1}^{3}y^mH_{6-2m,m}(X;z_0,z_1),
\]

where the subscripts record the degrees in the ternary and binary blocks. Indeed, a monomial with \(y\)-exponent \(k\) and binary degree \(\ell\) is invariant exactly when \(k-\ell\equiv0\pmod6\). With \(k+\ell\le6\), this gives \(k=\ell=0,1,2,3\) and the two pure degree-six cases. The coefficient dimension is

\[
28+1+7+15\cdot2+6\cdot3+4=88.
\]

**Cyclic-six support theorem.** Every smooth member \(X_F=V(F)\) satisfies

\[
H^4(X_F,\mathbb Q)^\tau\subseteq N^1H^4(X_F,\mathbb Q).
\]

**Proof.** Smoothness forces \(a\ne0\), squarefreeness of \(P_6\), and smoothness of \(f_6=0\). If one condition failed, the corresponding coordinate point or plane would contain a singular point of \(F\): all omitted transverse first derivatives vanish there. Thus

\[
C=\{P_6(\alpha,\beta)=aZ^6\}\subset\mathbb P^2
\]

is a smooth integral curve. Over its affine chart \(Z=1\), consider the family of sextic threefolds

\[
V_{\alpha,\beta}:
f_6(X)+a(y^6+T^6)
 +\sum_{m=1}^{3}(yT)^mH_{6-2m,m}(X;\alpha,\beta)=0
\quad\text{in }\mathbb P^4_{X,y,T}.
\]

It maps to \(X_F\) by

\[
p(X,y,T;\alpha,\beta)=(X,y,\alpha T,\beta T).
\]

This map has degree six: over a general target point, \(T^6=P_6(z_0,z_1)/a\). Its generic fiber over \(C\) is a smooth, geometrically integral threefold. Indeed, it is a base change of a general hyperplane section in the pencil \([z_0:z_1]\). The pencil base \(f_6(X)+ay^6=0\) in \(\mathbb P^3\) is smooth, and its nonzero core gradient makes every pencil member smooth along the base. Bertini gives smoothness elsewhere; connectedness of ample hyperplane sections gives geometric integrality.

On this cover define

\[
\begin{aligned}
d &: (X,y,T;\alpha,\beta)
 \longmapsto(X,y,\zeta T;\zeta^{-1}\alpha,\zeta^{-1}\beta),\\
\sigma &: (X,y,T;\alpha,\beta)
 \longmapsto(X,T,y;\alpha,\beta),\\
r &: (X,y,T;\alpha,\beta)
 \longmapsto(X,-y,-T;\alpha,\beta),\\
e=\sigma d\sigma &: (X,y,T;\alpha,\beta)
 \longmapsto(X,\zeta y,T;\zeta^{-1}\alpha,\zeta^{-1}\beta).
\end{aligned}
\]

Homogeneity verifies that they preserve the equation and that

\[
pd=p,\qquad pe=gp,\qquad pr=\tau p,
\qquad r=d^3e^3,\qquad r\sigma=\sigma r.
\]

The independent multipliers of \(y,T\) make \(\langle d,e\rangle\cong(\mathbb Z/6)^2\), and \(\sigma\) exchanges these two factors. The group is therefore the finite semidirect product \((\mathbb Z/6)^2\rtimes\mathbb Z/2\), of order 72. Compactify and resolve the cover and its projection equivariantly under this finite group. The resulting smooth projective fourfold \(\mathcal V\), its degree-six morphism \(p\), and the displayed actions meet the algebraic hypotheses of the deck/exchange criterion.

We check its two quotient hypotheses. First, \(r,\sigma\) fix the parameter curve. On a smooth general fiber their invariant ring in \(y,T\) is generated by

\[
S=y^2+T^2,\qquad P=yT,
\]

and the quotient equation is

\[
f_6(X)+a(S^3-3SP^2)
 +\sum_{m=1}^{3}P^mH_{6-2m,m}(X;\alpha,\beta)=0
\quad\text{in }\mathbb P(1^3,2^2).
\]

Its Fano property follows directly from the finite quotient. The smooth sextic threefold \(V\subset\mathbb P^4\) has \(K_V=\mathcal O_V(1)\). The only divisorial ramification of \(\pi:V\to V/\langle r,\sigma\rangle\) is along \(y=T\) and \(y=-T\), each a hyperplane section of ramification index two; \(r\) has no divisorial fixed locus. Hurwitz gives

\[
\pi^*(-K_{V/\langle r,\sigma\rangle})=\mathcal O_V(1).
\]

The quotient is normal with quotient singularities and ample rational anticanonical divisor. Its general fibers are therefore uniruled. A smooth projective model of the total quotient \(\mathcal V/\langle r,\sigma\rangle\) is uniruled as well, so Chapter 3's covering-curve theorem supports its entire fourth cohomology.

For the second quotient, choose any of the six simple projective roots of \(P_6\). It gives a fixed point of \(g\) on \(X_F\) with \(X=y=0\). In a chart with a nonzero binary coordinate, the three \(X\)-directions have eigenvalue \(\zeta\), the \(y\)-direction has eigenvalue \(\zeta^2\), and the binary-ratio direction has eigenvalue one. The simple-root derivative eliminates this last direction from the tangent space to \(X_F\). Hence the tangent age is

\[
\operatorname{age}(g)=\frac{1+1+1+2}{6}=\frac56<1.
\]

Since \(X_F\) is smooth projective with trivial canonical bundle, [Kollár–Larsen, Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701466) makes \(X_F/\langle g\rangle\) uniruled. Its smooth projective models also have divisor-supported fourth cohomology. Both quotient hypotheses now hold, and the deck/exchange criterion proves the theorem. ∎

This family is not contained in the quadratic-net family in the \(Y\) orientation. For a general member, its bidegree-\((4,2)\) contraction has image \(\langle yz_0,yz_1\rangle\). No basepoint-free three-dimensional net can contain this pencil: on \(y=0\), both forms vanish and any third homogeneous quadric has a projective zero. The net theorem and the present deck/exchange theorem therefore have distinct hypotheses.

### Paired signs and a surface quotient

Let \(P\) be generated by the paired signs \(s_i:(X_i,Y_i)\mapsto(-X_i,-Y_i)\), and let
\[
h=\operatorname{diag}(\zeta^2,\zeta,1,\zeta^3,\zeta^2,\zeta),
\qquad \zeta^6=1.
\]
Projectively \(P\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2\), since \(s_0s_1s_2\) is scalar. Its intersection with \(\langle h\rangle\) is trivial, and \(\tau=s_1h^3\). Thus \(\Gamma=P\times\langle h\rangle\) has order 24 and contains the prescribed involution. The \(\Gamma\)-invariant sextics form a 26-coefficient space: a monomial exponent \(e\) satisfies \(e_i+e_{i+3}\equiv0\pmod2\) for each pair and has \(h\)-weight zero modulo six. These conditions also imply global \(Y\)-evenness.

**Paired-sign sector theorem.** Suppose \(F\) lies in this space and \(X=V(F)\) is smooth. If the surface \(S\) over the passive field defined below is geometrically smooth, then
\[
H^4(X,\mathbb Q)^\Gamma\subseteq N^1H^4(X,\mathbb Q).
\]
The surface-smoothness condition holds on a nonempty open of the coefficient space. The supported primitive sector has Hodge dimensions \((22,74,22)\), hence rank 118; the ambient class raises the invariant rank to 119.

**The quotient field.** On the coordinate open put
\[
[u_0:u_1:u_2]=[X_0^2:X_1^2:X_2^2],\qquad
v=Y_0/X_0,\qquad c_i=(Y_i/X_i)/v\quad(i=1,2).
\]
These generate the \(P\)-invariant function field. Substitution \(Y_i=vc_iX_i\), with \(c_0=1\), turns the sextic into a ternary cubic in the \(u_i\): the pair-degree conditions make every exponent of \(X_i\) even, and their total degree is six. Its coefficients are polynomials in \(v\) and the two parameters \(c_i\). The diagonal action fixes \(c_1,c_2\) and sends
\[
v\mapsto\zeta v,\qquad
(u_0,u_1,u_2)\mapsto(\zeta^4u_0,\zeta^2u_1,u_2).
\]
Quotienting also by \(\tau\) replaces \(v\) by \(b=v^2\). Over \(K=\mathbb C(c_1,c_2)\), homogenization gives
\[
S=\{H=0\}\subset\mathbb P^2_u\times\mathbb P^1_{(b:r)},
\qquad H=\sum_{j=0}^3 b^jr^{3-j}C_j(u).
\]
Here \(C_0,C_3\) lie in the span of \(u_0^3,u_1^3,u_2^3,u_0u_1u_2\), \(C_1\) in the span of \(u_0^2u_1,u_1^2u_2,u_2^2u_0\), and \(C_2\) in the span of \(u_0u_1^2,u_1u_2^2,u_2u_0^2\). In particular \(S\) has bidegree \((3,3)\). The remaining order-three action, with \(\omega=\zeta^2\), is
\[
\phi:(b:r;u_0:u_1:u_2)\mapsto
(\omega b:r;\omega^2u_0:\omega u_1:u_2).
\]
It preserves \(H\), and \(X/\Gamma\) is birational over the passive surface to the family \(T=S/\langle\phi\rangle\).

**The surface cohomology.** Adjunction and the hypersurface exact sequence give
\[
K_S=\mathcal O_S(0,1),\qquad q(S)=0,\qquad p_g(S)=2.
\]
For example, \(H^1(\mathcal O_S)=0\) follows from Künneth applied to \(\mathcal O(-3,-3)\), and the two canonical sections are represented on \(r=1\) by residues with numerators \(1,b\). The determinant of the action on \(u\) is one, while \(db\) has character \(\omega\). The two holomorphic forms therefore have characters \(\omega,\omega^2\).

The action is free. A fixed point would lie over \(b=0\) or \(r=0\) and at one of the three coordinate vertices in \(\mathbb P^2\). None is on \(S\): the six pure sixth-power coefficients are nonzero, since otherwise the corresponding coordinate vertex would be singular on \(X\). Thus \(T\) is smooth and
\[
p_g(T)=q(T)=0.
\]
It has \(\chi(\mathcal O_T)=1\) and \(b_2(T)=10\), since the free cover has degree three, \(\chi(\mathcal O_S)=3\), and \(K_S^2=0\). The surface-fibration theorem of §3.2 supports all fourth cohomology on a smooth projective model of \(X/\Gamma\). Quotient transfer proves the claimed support on \(X\).

Since \(S\to T\) is étale, \(K_S\) is the pullback of \(K_T\), and \(T\) has Kodaira dimension one. Its genus-one fibration has multiple fibers of order three over the images of \(b=0,\infty\). The support input is the algebraicity of \(H^2(T)\); this example shows why the surface-fibration theorem also applies beyond uniruled fibers. The quotient construction follows the [surface-quotient argument of `hodgepodgeconjecture`](https://github.com/hodge-computer/sextics/discussions/55#discussioncomment-19077807).

**Openness and dimensions.** At the Fermat member,
\[
H=\sum_{i=0}^2(r^3+c_i^6b^3)u_i^3,\qquad c_0=1.
\]
Choose nonzero \(c_i\) with distinct sixth powers. The zero sets of the three coefficients on \(\mathbb P^1\) are disjoint and reduced. At a putative singular point, the \(u\)-partials force all but one coordinate to vanish; the derivative of its nonzero coordinate's coefficient then excludes singularity. At \(b=0,\infty\), the fiber is a smooth diagonal cubic. Properness and openness of smoothness therefore give the required nonempty coefficient open. The theorem is stated with this condition; it does not infer it for every special member from smoothness of \(X\) alone.

The equivariant Koszul series is constant on the smooth coefficient locus, so the Hodge dimensions may be counted in the Fermat ring \(\mathbb C[Z]/(Z_0^5,\ldots,Z_5^5)\). The projective volume has \(h\)-weight nine, hence numerator weight three modulo six is required. The exact count is

```python
from itertools import product

w = (2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 1)
def character(e, weight):
    return (all((e[i]+e[i+3]) % 2 == 0 for i in range(3))
            and sum(a*b for a, b in zip(e, w)) % 6 == weight)

assert sum(sum(e) == 6 and character(e, 0)
           for e in product(range(7), repeat=6)) == 26
assert [sum(sum(e) == d and character(e, 3)
            for e in product(range(5), repeat=6))
        for d in (6, 12, 18)] == [22, 74, 22]
```

These are the \((3,1),(2,2),(1,3)\) dimensions of the primitive representation. The normal-form projective dimension is 25. Its block-linear saturation has dimension 37: the diagonal six-dimensional torus preserves the coefficient space and the twelve off-diagonal Fermat orbit derivatives lie outside it. The corresponding quotient dimension is 20. The representation has rank 118, compared with rank 1282 for the full invariant primitive cohomology.

## 4.3 Cyclic-seven symmetry

Let \(\sigma\) act on \((x,y,z)=(X_0,X_1,X_2)\) with weights \((1,2,4)\) modulo seven and fix \(Y\). The complete \(\sigma\)-invariant, \(Y\)-even sextic family is

\[
F=a\cdot x^{5}\cdot y+b\cdot y^{5}\cdot z+c\cdot z^{5}\cdot x+d\cdot x^{2}\cdot y^{2}\cdot z^{2}+x\cdot y^{3}\cdot Q_{0}(Y)+x^{3}\cdot z\cdot Q_{1}(Y)+y\cdot z^{3}\cdot Q_{2}(Y)+g(Y).
\]

where \(Q_i\) are arbitrary ternary quadratics and \(g\) is an arbitrary ternary sextic. This is a fifty-dimensional coefficient space.

**Cyclic-seven sector theorem.** Every smooth member of this family has \(H^4(X)^{\tau,\sigma}\subset N^1H^4(X)\). Its invariant primitive Hodge numbers are \((19,128,19)\).

**Proof.** Introduce the rational coordinates

\[
\begin{gathered}
U=x^{2}\cdot y/z,     V=y^{2}\cdot z/x,     W=z^{2}\cdot x/y,\\
p=aU^{2}W+bV^{2}U+cW^{2}V+dUVW,\\
P=p+UVQ_{0}+UWQ_{1}+VWQ_{2}+g.
\end{gathered}
\]

Substitution gives \(F=P\). The target is the weighted fourfold \(\mathcal W=\{P=0\}\subset \mathbb P(2,2,2,1,1,1)\). On a chart \(Y_{j}=1\) and \(x\cdot y\cdot z\ne0\), the exponent matrix for \((x,y,z)\mapsto (U,V,W)\) is

\[
\begin{gathered}
\begin{pmatrix}2&1&-1\\-1&2&1\\1&-1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det=14.
\end{gathered}
\]

Its kernel consists of \(\sigma \) and the simultaneous sign change of \(x,y,z\), the latter being \(\tau \) projectively on this chart. Thus the rational map has degree fourteen and identifies the function field of \(\mathcal W\) with the invariant function field of \(X\). The full inverse image of \(P=0\) is \(F=0\), which is irreducible because a reducible projective hypersurface of this dimension is singular along an intersection of components.

We check quasismoothness on every coordinate stratum. Smoothness of \(F\) implies smoothness of its plane restrictions \(F(X,0)\) and \(g(Y)\), because derivatives in the omitted coordinates vanish there. It also forces \(ab\cdot c\ne0\) by examining the three \(X\)-coordinate points. On \(U\cdot V\cdot W\ne 0\), the coordinate map is étale, with Jacobian \(14\cdot x\cdot y\cdot z\), so a singular cone point of \(P\) would lift to one of \(F\). If \(U=0\) and \(V\cdot W\ne 0\), then \(P_V=W(cW+Q_{2})\) and \(P_W=V(2\cdot cW+Q_{2})\); these cannot both vanish. The other two such strata follow cyclically. If \(U\ne 0,V=W=0\), the equation reduces to \(g=0\): for \(Y\ne 0\) use \(\nabla g\ne 0\), while for \(Y=0\) use \(P_W=aU^{2}\ne 0\). Treat the \(V\)-only and \(W\)-only strata in the same way. If \(U=V=W=0\), use smoothness of \(g\) once more. These exhaust the nonzero cone points.

The singular locus of the weighted ambient space meets \(\mathcal W\) along the smooth plane cubic \(p=0\) at \(Y=0\). Transversely the singularities are \(\frac12(1,1,1)\), since the three \(Y\) directions are the odd stabilizer directions. Their age is \(\frac32\), so they are terminal. Weighted adjunction gives \(-K_\mathcal W=\mathcal O(3)\). The normal-Fano support theorem of Chapter 3 gives divisor-supported \(H^4\) on a resolution. Quotient transfer then supports \(H^4(X)^{\tau,\sigma}\), including the boundary terms introduced when resolving the rational map. ∎

**Character dimensions.** The residue volume is invariant under \(\sigma\) and anti-invariant under \(\tau\). The corresponding degree-six numerator space is

\[
x\cdot y\cdot z\cdot k[Y_{0},Y_{1},Y_{2}]_{3} \oplus  \operatorname{span}\{x^{3}\cdot y^{2},y^{3}\cdot z^{2},z^{3}\cdot x^{2}\}\cdot k[Y_{0},Y_{1},Y_{2}]_{1}.
\]

There are \(10+9=19\) directions. The degree-six odd Jacobian generators \(Y_jF_{X_i}\) and \(X_iF_{Y_j}\) have nonzero \(\sigma\)-characters \(-w_i\) and \(w_i\), with \(w_i\in\{1,2,4\}\). None of the nineteen invariant directions is therefore Jacobian-trivial.

For completeness, all character dimensions here follow from one explicit Koszul series. In the ring with \(u^{7}=v^{2}=1\), take the coefficient of \(t^{6\cdot q}\cdot u^{0}\cdot v^{1}\) in

\[
\begin{gathered}
\prod _{i} (1-t^{5}\cdot u^{-w_{i}}v^{e_{i}})/(1-t\cdot u^{w_{i}}v^{e_{i}}),\\
w=(1,2,4,0,0,0),     e=(0,0,0,1,1,1).
\end{gathered}
\]

At \(q=1\) it is 19; at \(q=2\) it is \(395-276+9=128\), the three terms being the polynomial, first Koszul and second Koszul contributions. Hodge symmetry gives \((19,128,19)\). The same monomial count in \(S_6\) gives fifty coefficients. Diagonal \(X\) changes and all \(Y\) changes preserve the family, so its projective saturation has dimension at most \(49+6=55\). At the smooth split Klein member, the six off-diagonal \(X\) orbit derivatives are nonzero and have the six distinct nontrivial \(\sigma\)-characters. They supply six independent directions outside the invariant family, proving equality. The member is smooth: a zero coordinate at a common zero of the ternary Klein gradient forces all coordinates to vanish; on the coordinate torus, multiplying its three derivative equations gives \(1=(-5)^3\), a contradiction. Thus the family has projective dimension 49 and saturated dimension 55, while the supported primitive representation has rank 166.

## 4.4 A generic support criterion

Here “generic” refers to the geometric generic point of the full even-sextic parameter space. A support defined there spreads to a finite-type family dominating that space; the dominance hypothesis is essential to the deformation argument.
